6 Introduction  
 
Purpose and Basis 
 of Valuation 
The Valuation has been prepared for a Regulated Purpose as defined in the RICS Valuation 
– Global Standards and the UK national supplement current as at the Valuation Date ( the 
“Red Book”). 
We understand that our valuation report and the Appendices to it (together the “Valuation 
Report”) are required for inclusion in a p rospectus (the “Prospectus”) which is to be 
published by the Company pursuant to a proposed listing and admission of the Company’s 
ordinary shares to the standard segment of the Official List of the FCA and to trading on the 
standard segment of the Main Market of the London Stock Exchange (the “Transaction”). 
The effective date of valuation is 31 December 2022. 
In accordance with the Red Book we have made certain disclosures in connection with this 
valuation instruction and our relationship with the Addressees. 
Market Value  We are of the opinion that the Market Va lues of the subject Properties are as shown below 
and as more particularly set out in Appendix A. 
All the Properties are held freehold-equivalent.  There are no negative values to report. 
For the avoidance of doubt, we have valued the unencumbered freehold-equivalent interests 
in the real estate and have not taken any into account outstanding purchase payments (or 
any part-payments already made) or profit-sharing provisions.  The market values reported 
herein do not represent valuations of the Company’s contractual rights.

Market Conditions –

accordance with the definition set out herein as at the date of valuation.   Amongst other

7 Introduction

We would draw your attention to the fact that a combination of global inflationary pressures 
(leading to higher interest rates), currency movements  and the current war in Ukraine has 
heightened the potential for greater volatility in property markets over the short -to-medium 
term.  
Past experience has shown that consumer and investor behaviour can quickly change during 
periods of such heightened volatility.   You should note that the conclusions set out in this 
report are only  valid as at the valuation date. Where appropriate, we would recommend 
that the valuation is closely monitored, as we continue to track how market participants 
respond to current market volatility.  
Portfolios and 
Aggregation 
We have valued the Properties individually and no account has been taken of any discount 
or premium that may be negotiated in the market if all or part of the portfolio was to be 
marketed simultaneously, either in lots or as a whole. 
SVPs, JVs and Other 
Indirect Investment 
Structures 
Where a property is owned through a special purpose  vehicle (SVP), joint venture (JV) or 
other indirect investment structure, our valuation  represents the 100% value of the whole 
property valued as real estate, assuming full management control. Our valuation therefore 
is unlikely to represent the market value of the interests in the indirect investment structure 
through which the property is held. 
Our Valuation does not necessarily represent the ‘Fair Value’ in accordance with IFRS 13 or 
FRS102 of the interests in the indirect investment structure through which the property is 
held. 
Outstanding Purchase 
Payments 
From information provided as at 30 September 2022, under the development and purchase 
contracts entered into by Dar Al Arkan, there are outstanding purchase payments as follows: 
W Residences, UAE:  AED 150,000,000 
Les Vagues, Qater:  QAR  322,481,842 (100% price) 
Aida, Oman:  OMR 63,442,479 + OMR 5,155,177 on sale of hotel. 
We have not taken these future payments into account in our valuations. 
Profit-Sharing 
Provisions  
From information provided, under the development and purchase contracts entered into by 
Dar Al Arkan, there are profit-sharing provisions in favour of the current owners / partners  
as follows: 
W Residences, UAE:  50% 
Les Vages, Qatar:  30% 
Aida, Oman:  25%. 
We have not taken these profit-sharing obligations into account in our valuations. 
Valuation Approach 
for Properties Held for 
or in Course of 
Development 
The Properties have been valued on either the Comparable Method (where appropriate) or 
the Residual (Development Appraisal) Method, or both approaches have been considered 
as cross-checks.   
The residual method is the commonly practised method of valuing development property, 
whereby the estimated total costs of realising the proposed development (including 
construction costs, fees and other on-costs, contingencies, costs of finance and developer’s 
profit) are deducted from the gross development value of the completed project to determine 
the residual value.  Where the residual method of valuation is used, we should draw your 
attention to the fact that this approach is very sensitive to changes in key inputs. S mall 
changes in variables such as sales volumes or build costs will have a disproportionate effect 
on residual or land value as demonstrated in the sensitivity analyses below. Residual values 
can therefore be susceptible to considerable variances as a resu lt of changes in market 
conditions. 
Whilst we have checked the information provided to us against available sources of 
information and provided for a level of profit which in our opinion reflects the level of risk 
inherent in each project, unforeseen event s such as delays in timing, minor market

the input variables adopted, then the value reported is subject to change and we reserve 
the right to amend our valuation figures accordingly. 
Report Format Appendix A of this Valuation Report provides the Property Details and Market Values of the 
Properties. Appendix B provides a table of information provided to CBRE by Dar Al Arkan.  
 
Compliance with  
Valuation Standards 
The Valuation has been prepared in accordance with the latest version of the RICS Valuation 
– Global Standards (incorporating the International Valua tion Standards) and the UK 
national supplement (the “Red Book”) current as the Valuation Date.  
The valuations are compliant with the International Valuation Standards and the London 
Stock Exchange requirements.   
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has published technical note 'Primary Market TN 
619.1' to replace and incorporate the ESMA update (ESMA/2011/81) of the Committee of 
European Securities Regulators’ (CESR) recommendations for the consistent implementation 
of the European Commission regulation (EC) n. 809/2004 into UK law ("TN 619.1") and, 
although this does not form part of the UK’s EU  Retained Law, the FCA expects Issuers to 
apply the provisions to the extent relevant. Accordingly, the valuation report is also compliant 
with paragraphs 128 to 130 (inclusive) of Part III.1 (Property companies) of TN 619.1. 
The Properties have been valued by a valuer who is qualified for the purpose of the Valuation 
in accordance with the Red Book. We confirm that we have sufficient local and national 
knowledge of the particular property market involved and have the skills and understanding 
to undertake the Valuation competently.  
Where the knowledge and skill requirements of the Red Book have been met in aggregate 
by more than one valuer within CBRE, we confirm that a list of those valuers has been 
retained within the working papers, together with confirmation that each named valuer 
complies with the requirements of the Red Book.  
This Valuation is a professional opinion and is expressly not intended to serve as a warranty, 
assurance or guarantee of any particular value of the subject Properties.  Other valuers may 
reach different conclusions as to the value of the subject Properties. This Valuation is for the 
sole purpose of providing the intended user with the valuer’s independent professional 
opinion of the value of the subject Properties as at the Valuation Date. 
Sustainability 
Considerations 
Wherever appropriate, sustainability and environmental matters are an integral part of the 
valuation approach. ‘Sustainability’ is taken to mean the consideration of such matters as 
environment and cl imate change, health and well -being and corporate responsibility that 
can or do impact on the valuation of an asset. In a valuation context, sustainability 
encompasses a wide range of physical, social, environmental, and economic factors that 
can affect va lue. The range of issues includes key environmental risks, such as flooding, 
energy efficiency and climate, as well as matters of design, configuration, accessibility, 
legislation, management, and fiscal considerations – and current and historic land use.  
Sustainability has an impact on the value of an asset, even if not explicitly recognised. 
Valuers reflect markets, they do not lead them. Where we recognise the value impacts of 
sustainability, we are reflecting our understanding of how market participant s include 
sustainability requirements in their bids and the impact on market valuations. 
Assumptions The Property Details on which each Valuation is based are as set out in this report. We have 
made various assumptions as to tenure, letting, taxation, town planning, and the condition 
and repair of buildings and sites – including ground and groundwater contamination – as 
set out below.

Sources of 
Information 
We have carried out our work based upon information supplied to us Dar Al Arkan  and their

 We have included a schedule in Appendix B of the information provided to us by Dar Al Arkan

Legal due diligence reports, technical due diligence reports, environmental due diligence

14 Valuation Assumptions  
 
Introduction An Assumption is defined in the Red Book Glossary and VPS 4 to be a “supposition taken to 
be true” (an “Assumption”). 
Assumptions are facts, conditions or situations affecting the subject of, or approach to, a 
valuation that it has been agreed need not be verified by the valuer as part of the valuation 
process.  Assumptions are made when it is reasonable for the valuer to accept that something 
is true without the need for specific investigation. 
Dar Al Arkan  and the Company ha ve confirmed and we confirm that our Assumptions are 
correct as far as Dar Al Arkan, the Company and we, respectively, are aware.  In the event that 
any of these Assumptions prove to be incorrect then our valuations should be reviewed.  The 
principal Assumptions which we have made are stated within this Valuation Report.   
For the avoidance of doubt, the Assumptions made do not affect compliance with the approach 
to Market Value under the Red Book. 
Capital Values Each valuation has been prepared on the basis of “Market Value”), which is defined in the Red 
Book as: 
“The estimated amount for which an asset or liability should exchange on the Valuation Date  
between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s length transaction, after proper 
marketing and where the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently and without 
compulsion.” 
The Valuation represents the figure that would appear in a hypothetical contract of sale at the 
Valuation Date. No adjustment has been made to this figure for any expenses of acquisition or 
realisation - nor for taxation which might arise in the event of a disposal. 
No account has been taken of any inter -company leases or arrangements, nor of any 
mortgages, debentures or other charge. 
No account has been taken of  the availability or otherwise of capital based Government or 
European Community grants. 
Taxation, Costs and 
Realisation Costs 
As stated above, no allowances have been made for any expenses of realisation nor for taxation 
which might arise in the event of a disposal.   
 Our valuations reflect purchasers' statutory and other normal acquisition costs. 
VAT or Equivalent We have not been advised whether the properties are elected for VAT or equivalent taxes. 
 All rents and capital values stated in this report are exclusive of VAT or equivalent taxes. 
Passing Rent Passing rents quoted in this report are the rents which are currently payable under the terms of 
the leases.  Passing rents exclude service charges and VAT and are prior to deduction of any 
non-recoverable costs.  Passing rents exclude turnover rents, mall incomes and other 
miscellaneous incomes. 
Net Annual Rent Net annual rent is defined for the purposes of this transaction as "the current income or income 
estimated by the valuer: 
 (i)   ignoring any special receipts or deduction arising from the property; 
 (ii)  excluding Value Added Tax and before taxation (including tax on profits and any allowances 
for interest on capital or loans); and 
 (iii)  after making deductions for superior rents (but not for amortisation), and any disbursements 
including, if appropriate, expenses of managing the property and allowances to maintain it in 
a condition to command its rent". 
Estimated Net 
Annual Rental Value 
The estimated net annual ren tal value is based on the current rental value of each of the 
Properties.  The rental value reflects the terms of the leases where the Properties, or parts 
thereof, are let at the date of valuation.  Where the Properties, or parts thereof, are vacant at 
the date of valuation, the rental value reflects the rent we consider would be obtainable on an 
open market letting as at the date of valuation.

15 Valuation Assumptions  
 
Rental Values Unless stated otherwise rental values indicated in our report are those which have been 
adopted by us as appropriate in assessing the capital value and are not necessarily appropriate 
for other purposes, nor do they necessarily accord with the definition of Market Rent in the Red 
Book, which is as follows: 
"The estimated amount for which an interest in real property should be leased on the Valuation 
Date between a willing lessor and a willing lessee on appropriate lease terms in an arm's length 
transaction, after proper marketing and where the parties had each acted knowledgeably, 
prudently and without compulsion." 
Fixtures, Fittings 
and Equipment 
Where appropriate we have regarded the shop fronts of retail and showroom accommodation 
as forming an integral part of the building. 
Landlord’s fixtures such as lifts, escalators, central heating and other normal service 
installations have been treated as an integral part of the building and are included within our 
Valuations. 
Process plant and machinery, tenants’ fixtures and specialis t trade fittings have been excluded 
from our Valuations. 
All measurements, areas and ages quoted in our report are approximate. 
Environmental 
Matters 
In the absence of any information to the contrary, we have assumed that: 
a) the Properties are not contaminated and are not adversely affected by any existing or 
proposed environmental law; 
b) any processes which are carried out on the Properties  which are regulated by 
environmental legislation are properly licensed by the appropriate authorities; 
c) the Properties will comply with relevant energy performance legislation.   
d) the Properties are either not subject to flooding risk or, if it is, that sufficient flood

Development 
The Properties have been valued on either the Comparable Method (where appropriate) or 
the Residual (Development Appraisal) Method, or both approaches have been considered 
as cross-checks.   
The residual method is the commonly practised method of valuing development property, 
whereby the estimated total costs of realising the proposed development (including 
construction costs, fees and other on-costs, contingencies, costs of finance and developer’s 
profit) are deducted from the gross development value of the completed project to determine 
the residual value.  Where the residual method of valuation is used, we should draw your 
attention to the fact that this approach is very sensitive to changes in key inputs. S mall 
changes in variables such as sales volumes or build costs will have a disproportionate effect 
on residual or land value as demonstrated in the sensitivity analyses below. Residual values 
can therefore be susceptible to considerable variances as a resu lt of changes in market 
conditions. 
Whilst we have checked the information provided to us against available sources of 
information and provided for a level of profit which in our opinion reflects the level of risk 
inherent in each project, unforeseen event s such as delays in timing, minor market

Sustainability 
Considerations 
Wherever appropriate, sustainability and environmental matters are an integral part of the 
valuation approach. ‘Sustainability’ is taken to mean the consideration of such matters as 
environment and cl imate change, health and well -being and corporate responsibility that 
can or do impact on the valuation of an asset. In a valuation context, sustainability 
encompasses a wide range of physical, social, environmental, and economic factors that 
can affect va lue. The range of issues includes key environmental risks, such as flooding, 
energy efficiency and climate, as well as matters of design, configuration, accessibility, 
legislation, management, and fiscal considerations – and current and historic land use.  
Sustainability has an impact on the value of an asset, even if not explicitly recognised. 
Valuers reflect markets, they do not lead them. Where we recognise the value impacts of 
sustainability, we are reflecting our understanding of how market participant s include 
sustainability requirements in their bids and the impact on market valuations.

Introduction An Assumption is defined in the Red Book Glossary and VPS 4 to be a “supposition taken to 
be true” (an “Assumption”). 
Assumptions are facts, conditions or situations affecting the subject of, or approach to, a 
valuation that it has been agreed need not be verified by the valuer as part of the valuation 
process.  Assumptions are made when it is reasonable for the valuer to accept that something 
is true without the need for specific investigation. 
Dar Al Arkan  and the Company ha ve confirmed and we confirm that our Assumptions are 
correct as far as Dar Al Arkan, the Company and we, respectively, are aware.  In the event that 
any of these Assumptions prove to be incorrect then our valuations should be reviewed.  The 
principal Assumptions which we have made are stated within this Valuation Report.   
For the avoidance of doubt, the Assumptions made do not affect compliance with the approach 
to Market Value under the Red Book. 
Capital Values Each valuation has been prepared on the basis of “Market Value”), which is defined in the Red 
Book as: 
“The estimated amount for which an asset or liability should exchange on the Valuation Date  
between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s length transaction, after proper 
marketing and where the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently and without 
compulsion.” 
The Valuation represents the figure that would appear in a hypothetical contract of sale at the 
Valuation Date. No adjustment has been made to this figure for any expenses of acquisition or 
realisation - nor for taxation which might arise in the event of a disposal. 
No account has been taken of any inter -company leases or arrangements, nor of any 
mortgages, debentures or other charge. 
No account has been taken of  the availability or otherwise of capital based Government or 
European Community grants. 
Taxation, Costs and 
Realisation Costs 
As stated above, no allowances have been made for any expenses of realisation nor for taxation 
which might arise in the event of a disposal.   
 Our valuations reflect purchasers' statutory and other normal acquisition costs. 
VAT or Equivalent We have not been advised whether the properties are elected for VAT or equivalent taxes. 
 All rents and capital values stated in this report are exclusive of VAT or equivalent taxes. 
Passing Rent Passing rents quoted in this report are the rents which are currently payable under the terms of 
the leases.  Passing rents exclude service charges and VAT and are prior to deduction of any 
non-recoverable costs.  Passing rents exclude turnover rents, mall incomes and other 
miscellaneous incomes. 
Net Annual Rent Net annual rent is defined for the purposes of this transaction as "the current income or income 
estimated by the valuer: 
 (i)   ignoring any special receipts or deduction arising from the property; 
 (ii)  excluding Value Added Tax and before taxation (including tax on profits and any allowances 
for interest on capital or loans); and 
 (iii)  after making deductions for superior rents (but not for amortisation), and any disbursements 
including, if appropriate, expenses of managing the property and allowances to maintain it in 
a condition to command its rent". 
Estimated Net 
Annual Rental Value 
The estimated net annual ren tal value is based on the current rental value of each of the 
Properties.  The rental value reflects the terms of the leases where the Properties, or parts 
thereof, are let at the date of valuation.  Where the Properties, or parts thereof, are vacant at 
the date of valuation, the rental value reflects the rent we consider would be obtainable on an 
open market letting as at the date of valuation.

We would draw your attention to the fact that a combination of global inflationary pressures 
(leading to higher interest rates), currency movements  and the current war in Ukraine has 
heightened the potential for greater volatility in property markets over the short -to-medium 
term..  
Past experience has shown that consumer and investor behaviour can quickly change during 
periods of such heightened volatility.   You should note that the conclusions set out in this 
report are only valid as at the valuation date.  Where appropriate, we would recommend 
that the valuation is closely monitored, as we continue to track how market participants 
respond to current market volatility.  
Portfolios and 
Aggregation 
We have valued the Properties individually and no account has been taken of any discount 
or premium that may be negotiated in the market if all or part of the portfolio was to be 
marketed simultaneously, either in lots or as a whole. 
SVPs, JVs and Other 
Indirect Investment 
Structures 
Where a property is owned through a special purpose  vehicle (SVP), joint venture (JV) or 
other indirect investment structure, our valuation  represents the 100% value of the whole 
property valued as real estate, assuming full management control. Our valuation therefore 
is unlikely to represent the market value of the interests in the indirect investment structure 
through which the property is held. 
Our Valuation does not necessarily represent the ‘Fair Value’ in accordance with IFRS 13 or 
FRS102 of the interests in the indirect investment structure through which the property is 
held. 
Valuation Approach 
for Properties Held for 
or in Course of 
Development 
The Properties have been valued on either the Comparable Method (where appropriate) or 
the Residual (Development Appraisal) Method , or both approaches have been considered 
as cross-checks.   
The residual method is the commonly practised method of valuing development property, 
whereby the estimated total costs of realising the proposed development (including 
construction costs, fees and other on-costs, contingencies, costs of finance and developer’s 
profit) are deducted from the gross development value of the completed project to determine 
the residual value.  Where the residual method of v aluation is used, we should draw your 
attention to the fact that this approach is very sensitive to changes in key inputs. Small 
changes in variables such as sales volumes or build costs will have a disproportionate effect 
on residual or land value as demonstrated in the sensitivity analyses below. Residual values 
can therefore be susceptible to considerable variances as a result of changes in market 
conditions. 
Whilst we have checked the information provided to us against available sources of 
information and provided for a level of profit which in our opinion reflects the level of risk 
inherent in each project, unforeseen events such as delays in timing, minor market 
movements etc. can have a disproportionate effect on the resulting value.  Land values have 
been benchmarked against comparable transactions where available and reflect our 
opinion as at the date of valuation.  Should information which we were not made aware of 
at the time of the valuation subsequently come to light which changes ou r view on any of 
the input variables adopted, then the value reported is subject to change and we reserve 
the right to amend our valuation figures accordingly.

opinion of the value of the subject Properties as at the Valuation Date. 
Sustainability 
Considerations 
Wherever appropriate, sustainability and environmental matters are an integral part of the 
valuation approach. ‘Sustainability’ is taken to mean the consideration of such matters as 
environment and cl imate change, health and well -being and corporate responsibility that 
can or do impact on the valuation of an asset. In a valuation context, sustainability 
encompasses a wide range of physical, social, environmental, and economic factors that 
can affect va lue. The range of issues includes key environmental risks, such as flooding, 
energy efficiency and climate, as well as matters of design, configuration, accessibility, 
legislation, management, and fiscal considerations – and current and historic land use.  
Sustainability has an impact on the value of an asset, even if not explicitly recognised. 
Valuers reflect markets, they do not lead them. Where we recognise the value impacts of 
sustainability, we are reflecting our understanding of how market participant s include 
sustainability requirements in their bids and the impact on market valuations. 
Assumptions The Property Details on which each Valuation is based are as set out in this report. We have 
made various assumptions as to tenure, letting, taxation, town planning, and the condition 
and repair of buildings and sites – including ground and groundwater contamination – as 
set out below.

found to be incorrect, the Valuation figures may also be incorrect and should be 
reconsidered.

15 Valuation Assumptions  
 
Introduction An Assumption is defined in the Red Book Glossary and VPS 4 to be a “supposition taken to 
be true” (an “Assumption”). 
Assumptions are facts, conditions or situations affecting the subject of, or approach to, a 
valuation that it has been agreed need not be verified by the valuer as part of the valuation 
process.  Assumptions are made when it is reasonable for the valuer to accept that something 
is true without the need for specific investigation. 
Dar Al Arkan  and the Company ha ve confirmed and we confirm that our Assumptions are 
correct as far as Dar Al Arkan, the Company and we, respectively, are aware.  In the event that 
any of these Assumptions prove to be incorrect then our valuations should be reviewed.  The 
principal Assumptions which we have made are stated within this Valuation Report.   
For the avoidance of doubt, the Assumptions made do not affect compliance with the approach 
to Market Value under the Red Book. 
Capital Values Each valuation has been prepared on the basis of “Market Value”, which is defined in the Red 
Book as: 
“The estimated amount for which an asset or liability should exchange on the Valuation Date 
between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s length transaction, after proper 
marketing and where the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently and without 
compulsion.” 
The Valuation represents the figure that would appear in a hypothetical contract of sale at the 
Valuation Date. No adjustment has been made to this figure for any expenses of acquisition or 
realisation - nor for taxation which might arise in the event of a disposal. 
No account has been taken of any inter -company leases or arrangements, nor of any 
mortgages, debentures or other charge. 
No account has been taken of the availability or otherwise of capital based Government or 
European Community grants. 
Taxation, Costs and 
Realisation Costs 
As stated above, no allowances have been made for any expenses of realisation nor for taxation 
which might arise in the event of a disposal.   
 Our valuations reflect purchasers' statutory and other normal acquisition costs. 
VAT or Equivalent We have not been advised whether the properties are elected for VAT or equivalent taxes. 
 All rents and capital values stated in this report are exclusive of VAT or equivalent taxes. 
Passing Rent Passing rents quoted in this report are the rents which are currently payable under the terms of 
the leases.  Passing rents exclude service charges and VAT and are prior to deduction of any 
non-recoverable costs.  Passing rents exclude turnover rents, mall incomes and other 
miscellaneous incomes. 
Net Annual Rent Net annual rent is defined for the purposes of this transaction as "the current income or income 
estimated by the valuer: 
 (i)   ignoring any special receipts or deduction arising from the property; 
 (ii)  excluding Value Added Tax and before taxation (including tax on profits and any allowances 
for interest on capital or loans); and 
 (iii)  after making deductions for superior rents (but not for amortisation), and any disbursements 
including, if appropriate, expenses of managing the property and allowances to maintain it in 
a condition to command its rent". 
Estimated Net 
Annual Rental Value 
The estimated net annual rental value is based on the current rental value of each of the 
Properties.  The rental value reflects the terms of the leases where the Propertie s, or parts 
thereof, are let at the date of valuation.  Where the Properties, or parts thereof, are vacant at 
the date of valuation, the rental value reflects the rent we consider would be obtainable on an 
open market letting as at the date of valuation.

Where a property is owned through a special purpose  vehicle (SVP), joint venture (JV) or

is unlikely to represent the market value of the interests in the indirect investment structure

the Residual (Development Appraisal) Method , or both approaches have been considered

The residual method is the commonly practised method of valuing development property, 
whereby the estimated total costs of realising the proposed development (including 
construction costs, fees and other on-costs, contingencies, costs of finance and developer’s 
profit) are deducted from the gross development value of the completed project to determine 
the residual value.  Where the residual method of v aluation is used, we should draw your 
attention to the fact that this approach is very sensitive to changes in key inputs. Small 
changes in variables such as sales volumes or build costs will have a disproportionate effect 
on residual or land value as demonstrated in the sensitivity analyses below. Residual values 
can therefore be susceptible to considerable variances as a result of changes in market 
conditions. 
Whilst we have checked the information provided to us against available sources of 
information and provided for a level of profit which in our opinion reflects the level of risk 
inherent in each project, unforeseen events such as delays in timing, minor market 
movements etc. can have a disproportionate effect on the resulting value.  Land values have 
been benchmarked against comparable transactions where available and reflect our 
opinion as at the date of valuation.  Should information which we were not made aware of 
at the time of the valuation subsequently come to light which changes ou r view on any of

ANTI-MONEY  
LAUNDERING 
POLICY

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
01. Introduction 
1.1 The Company (as defined in 3.1 below) has a zero-
tolerance approach towards Money Laundering and Terrorist 
Financing (both as defined in 4.1 below) and is committed 
to preventing Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in 
accordance with all applicable laws in countries where the 
Company operates.
1.2 The Company is committed to evaluating and upholding 
this Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Policy (“AML Policy”), 
together with its procedures and controls on an on-going 
ANTI-MONEY 
LAUNDERING POLICY
basis. The principles and standards as set out in this AML 
Policy are based on relevant laws and guidance, as well as a 
risk analysis. If these change materially, the AML Policy will 
be updated. Otherwise, and in all cases, the AML Policy will be 
reviewed on an annual basis.
1.3 Money laundering is how criminals change money and other 
assets into clean money or assets that have no obvious link to 
their criminal origins.
Page 2

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
02. Purpose
2.1 This AML Policy sets out the Company’s approach to 
preventing Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing 
by meeting the relevant standards on combatting Money 
Laundering and Terrorism Financing. 
2.2 This AML Policy takes into consideration the following 
pillars of an effective AML program to ensure compliance 
of all its Regulated Entities (as defined below): 
a) Compliance with applicable laws and industry guidance;
b) Identifying Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing 
risks and performing risk assessments;
c) Establishing and maintaining risk-based customer due 
diligence (CDD);
d) Establishing enhanced due diligence (EDD) for 
customers presenting a higher risk;
e) Appointment by each Regulated Entity of a money 
laundering reporting officer and their deputies where 
needed, hereinafter referred to as “MLRO” and entrusting 
roles and responsibilities to combat instances of Money 
Laundering. Regulated Entity means a Company which is 
required by local AML regulations to be registered before 
an AML local authority;
f) Establishing and maintaining risk-based systems and 
procedures for the ongoing monitoring of transactions, 
customers and activities of the Company;
g) Establishing procedures for reporting suspicious activity 
internally and, if necessary, escalation to the relevant law 
enforcement authorities;
h) Localisation of procedures to adhere to local laws;
i) Maintaining appropriate records; and
j) Providing adequate AML training to staff.
03. Scope
3.1 This AML Policy applies to: 
a) Dar Global PLC (Dar Global or we or us) and its 
subsidiaries and any future overseas subsidiaries from 
time to time and ultimately form part of the overall 
ownership/consolidation of a Dar Global (each a Group 
Company or the Company, and collectively referred to as 
the Dar Global Group), and;
b) all directors, officers, and employees, including all 
consultants, agents, brokers, contractors, seconded staff 
and casual workers wherever
3.2 All Employees of the Company shall familiarise 
themselves with the provisions of this AML Policy and 
implementing controls, and the following departments 
play a key role in ensuring compliance with this AML Policy: 
Finance & Accounts, Legal, Compliance, Procurement and 
Sales & Business Development.
3.3 The Company will take reasonable steps to require 
its counterparties to comply with this AML Policy or 
equivalent standards.
3.4 The procedures established in this AML Policy will be 
localised by the Head of Compliance with the support of 
the MLRO to comply with local minimum requirements 
as determined by applicable law and regulations in each 
jurisdiction where the Company operates (AML Localised 
Procedures Guideline).
Page 3

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
04. Money Laundering
4.1 The definitions of money laundering and terrorist 
financing differ in different jurisdictions, but in broad 
terms money laundering refers to the acquisition, dealing 
with, or agreement to deal with (or involvement in any 
transaction which facilitates the receipt of or dealing with) 
the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering). Proceeds 
of Crime include all property (including money) that 
you know or suspect is or represents (fully or partially) 
a benefit (direct or indirectly) from criminal conduct. 
Terrorist financing involves the solicitation, collection or 
provision of funds with the intention that they may be 
used to support terrorist acts or organizations (Terrorist 
Financing).
4.2 This AML Policy prohibits all Money Laundering and 
Terrorist Financing. The consequences of non-compliance 
with this AML Policy and relevant applicable laws may 
include imprisonment, fines and/or loss of employment as 
listed below:
4.3 For the Company:
a. criminal liabilities including unlimited fines;
b. confiscation orders;
c. serious reputational damage including media comment; 
d. unenforceability of contracts entered into due to 
illegality
4.4 For Employees:
a. personal criminal liability including fines and/or 
imprisonment;
b. confiscation orders;
c. disciplinary action initiated by the Company, including 
summary dismissal;
d. personal reputational damage; and
e. deportation, where applicable.
05. Regulatory Framework
5.1 The Company is committed to following international 
best practice, including UK regulations where applicable, 
such as the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA), 
international best practices in Anti-Money Laundering 
(AML) & Counter Terrorist Financing (CTF) and the 
Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 (SAMLA), 
Export Control Order 2008 , Counter-Terrorism Act 
2008, Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001 and 
the regulations, licences and guidance that relate to this 
legislation.
5.2 The regulators and government entities that enforce 
these laws expect companies to put in place risk-
based policies and procedures aimed at identifying 
risks of breaching AML and CTF laws and regulations 
and economic, financial or trade sanctions laws, 
export controls, regulations, directives, embargos, 
rules, mandatory guidelines, executive orders or similar 
restrictive measures (Sanctions).
5.3 Many countries in which the Company and its 
subsidiaries operate have enacted laws relating to Money 
Laundering and Terrorist Financing which the Company 
will follow as prescribed. In the
event of any inconsistency, the highest standard will 
generally apply, but you should speak to the MLRO for 
guidance in the case of uncertainty. These countries may 
also impose autonomous Sanctions that are different to 
those enacted and enforced by the Sanctions Authorities, 
and the Company will comply with those Sanctions where 
required.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 4

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
06. Money Laundering Reporting 
Officer & Suspicious Activity Report
6.1 Dar Global shall designate a MLRO for each Regulated 
Entity who has the responsibility of ensuring compliance 
with this AML Policy and implementing adequate 
procedures.
6.2 The Group Head of Compliance will be the MLRO’s 
point of contact for any support in fulfilling their 
responsibilities. MLROs and the Head of Compliance will 
have access to legal counsel from the Legal Department 
which shall in turn obtain external counsel if it deems 
necessary..
6.3 The MLRO will act in confidence as a point of 
escalation, provide guidance and clarifications regarding 
this AML Policy, and respond to any questions or enquiries
6.4 If the MLRO receives an internal suspicious activity 
report from an internal department (as per the form set 
out in Appendix D), he/she must, without delay:
a) investigate the circumstances in relation to which the 
report was made; and
b) determine, with the assistance of the legal function 
if the MLRO deems necessary, whether a corresponding 
external suspicious activity report (SAR) should be made 
to the external authorities and if required, make such an 
external report.
6.5 Responsibilities:
The MLRO’s responsibilities include, among others: 
a) Establishing and maintaining effective anti-Money 
Laundering policies, procedures, systems, and controls 
in compliance with applicable legislation according to 
jurisdictional nexus;
b) Assisting employees in their responsibility for complying 
with all relevant regulations, including the provision of 
advice on compliance issues, and acting as the point of 
contact to receive internal suspicious activity reports;
c) Handling any internal suspicious activity reports and taking 
appropriate actions following the receipt of such reports, 
including submitting external SARs to authorities, if required 
by relevant laws;
d) Reporting to Compliance on all relevant material or 
significant breaches and acting as the respective Regulated 
Entity’s point of contact for all external authorities regarding 
Money Laundering issues;
e) Responding promptly to any requests for information 
in relation to Money Laundering issues made by the local 
competent authorities;
f) Maintaining records of due process in line with the relevant 
local laws and this policy in order to respond to any requests 
for information from external authorities regarding Money 
Laundering issues]
g) Supporting and maintaining appropriate anti Money 
Laundering training programs and awareness arrangements; 
and
h) Oversight of know your client (KYC) procedure (as set out 
below).
6.6 Periodic Report
Unless required otherwise under Applicable Law, or triggered 
due to an event that requires immediate attention and 
rectification, the MLRO shall report to senior management on 
an annual basis the MLRO’s proposals for updates required 
to strengthen the Company’s AML compliance framework. 
The report shall also cover any significant breaches and 
other high-risk areas which require management attention. 
The MLRO will send a copy of the report to the relevant 
supervisory authority as required by applicable law.
6.7 Regulatory Co-operation
The MLRO/Head of Compliance shall be the point of contact 
in the Company as regards any communication with 
regulators and therefore, any correspondence received from 
regulators in respect of AML should be promptly forwarded to 
the MLRO/Head of Compliance.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 5

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
7. Risk Based Approach (RBA)
7.1 Customer Risk Assessments
Customer Risk Assessments must be conducted for 
all transactions involving a Regulated Entity. While it is 
essential that the Company complies with the legal and 
regulatory requirements placed upon it, the Company is 
permitted to adopt a risk-based approach in relation to 
Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing. This enables 
the Company to focus its efforts and resources on those 
situations that are of higher risk.
The factors that should be taken into account when 
considering the level of risk that a customer poses include, 
where a risk of Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing or 
Sanctions arise:
a) the jurisdiction in which the customer is registered / 
country of citizenship;
b) the country from which the customer operates;
c) the countries and geographical areas in which the 
customer does business;
d) the nature of the customer’s business and profile of its 
customers;
e) the source of funds of the customer;
f) whether or not, the customer (or a party to the 
transaction) falls within the legal definition of Politically 
Exposed Persons (PEPs).
For transactions with a Regulated Entity, be it the sales 
office or property location, the Sales Administration 
function shall, as part of the CDD process, obtain client 
KYC files and prepare a Client Risk Assessment Report as 
enclosed in Appendix C. For any clients that are rated high 
risk, the file will be submitted to the MLRO and Compliance 
department to conduct an EDD prior to clearance.
7.2 Customer or Counterparty Risk scoring
Guidance for CDD risk rating of customer risk 
subcategories, including geographical and business profiles 
is outlined below.
a) Low Risk:
Low risk customers are those individuals and entities 
whose identity and source of funds can be easily 
determined and whose account transactions by and large 
conform to their known profile. They may include the 
following (subject to a risk assessment):
i. Salaried employees (unless falling within one of the medium 
or high-risk categories below);
ii. Persons / entities registered in known ‘low risk’ jurisdictions;
iii. Persons / entities engaged in industry segments that do not 
make use of complex financial structures;
iv. Government departments/ government owned companies; 
regulators and statutory bodies etc. in low-risk jurisdictions;
v. Regulated banks, financial institutions, credit institutions, 
financial service providers, brokers that are regulated or listed 
or both; and
vi. Publicly listed entities in a low-risk jurisdiction which are 
subject to regulatory supervision.
b) Medium Risk:
Medium risk customers are categorized on the basis of 
their background, nature and location of activity, country of 
residence, sources of funds and customer profile. This could 
include (subject to a risk assessment):
i. High net worth individuals with known sources of income;
ii. PEPs, if acting as only a ‘sponsor’ of the Company;
iii. Persons / entities registered in known ‘medium risk’ 
jurisdictions
iv. Companies having closed family shareholding or beneficial 
ownership; and
v. Entities with silent partners who can be identified.
c) High Risk:
High risk customers typically include persons or corporate 
or associations or beneficial owners residing in high-risk 
countries as identified by any of the international bodies. This 
could include (subject to a risk assessment):
i. PEPs, if not acting as a ‘sponsor’ of the Company;
ii. Non-face to face customers or legal representative;
iii. Entities registered in or conducting business with high-risk 
jurisdictions;
iv. Persons with citizenship/residence in high-risk jurisdictions;
v. Persons / entities engaged in industry segments that are 
complex and/or particularly susceptible to AML risks;
vi. Persons with questionable reputation based on genuine 
-publicly available information;
vii. Trusts, charitable organizations, Non-government 
Organizations (NGOs); and
viii. Organizations receiving donations.

7.3 Business Risk Assessment
An effective and documented risk-based approach will enable 
the Company to justify its position on managing Money 
Laundering and terrorist risks to law enforcement, the courts, 
regulators, and supervisory bodies. The Company shall: 
a) Conduct on an annual basis a business risk assessment 
that considers its activities and structure and concludes on 
the Company’s exposure to Money Laundering and Terrorist 
Financing risk. In particular, the Company should consider its 
exposure to risks in relation to its customers, the jurisdictions 
in which it operates and its business.
b) Use the outcome of its business risk assessment to develop 
appropriate risk management systems and controls, and 
necessary updates to its policies and procedures.
7.4 Corporate customer related risks
The business risk assessment will include consideration of 
whether the corporate client:
a) acts for PEPs, particularly those located in jurisdictions with 
high levels of corruption;
b) acts for customers without meeting them i.e., non-face to 
face business
c) practices in locations with high levels of acquisitive crime, or 
for customers who have convictions for acquisitive crimes;
d) acts for customers affiliated to countries with high levels of 
corruption or organized crime, or where terrorist organizations 
operate, or countries with inadequate frameworks to prevent 
and detect Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing;
e) acts for entities that have complex ownership structures; 
and
f) acts for customers for which it cannot obtain details of the 
beneficial owners.
7.5 Real Estate and other Service Risk
The Company’s business risk assessment shall also consider 
different types of risk to which it might be exposed in relation 
to Money Laundering based on real estate structures including 
but not limited to:
a) the handling of cash or assets or through payments that 
are made to, or received from, unregulated third parties, 
particularly with a cross-border element;
b) use of corporate vehicles;
c) use of monetary instruments (including bearer negotiable 
instruments);
d) use of properties to conceal money generated by illegal 
activities; and
e) trusts or other structures that conceal the identities of the 
UBOs 
08. Customer Due Diligence (CDD)
8.1 Regulated Entities follow a KYC process to perform 
identity verification of all customers in accordance with 
applicable AML/CTF regulations, irrespective of the value of 
the transaction.
8.2 Regulated Entities will also ensure the legitimacy of the 
source of funds and the purpose of the transaction.
8.3 Regulated Entities shall maintain proof of identity / 
verification records, watch list and reputational risk search 
results for a minimum period of ten (10) years from the date 
the Regulated Entities ceases to have a relationship with the 
customer.
8.4 Customers are required to provide information in 
the Client Registration Form to their contact in the Sales 
Administration department prior to entering into any 
transactions with the Regulated Entities. The information 
collected shall be detailed in a form form based on the 
templates provided in this AML Policy Appendix – A (for 
individuals) and Appendix – B (for corporate entities), which 
may be adapted as necessary to reflect local regulatory 
requirements,.

8.5 Sanctions Screening  
The Company is committed to adhering to all relevant 
Sanctions adopted, administered or enforced by relevant 
sanctions authorities which may include (without limitation) 
those sanctions regimes administered and enforced by 
authorities including the United Kingdom, the U.S. Government 
(including, without limitation, the U.S. Department of the 
Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the U.S. 
Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Commerce), 
the European Union, or the Security Council of the United 
Nations (each of the foregoing, together with any other relevant 
regulatory authority, being a Sanctions Authority).
8.6 The Company is committed to ensuring that it does not, 
knowingly, do business with anyone whose name either 
appears on a Sanctions list (see 11 below). Clients who are from 
a country listed on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) list of 
Non-Cooperative Countries & Territories (NCCT), or any other 
country-specific list where the customer is operating shall 
have the highest risk rating for the geographic risk in the CDD 
assessment.
8.7 The Company will screen all prospective customers and 
customers in accordance with 11.3 below. Any commercial 
relationships or transactions that appear to involve (directly or 
indirectly) countries, entities, or individuals that are targeted by 
Sanctions must be brought to the attention of the MLRO before 
any action is taken.
8.8 Companies which are not Regulated Entities shall refer to 
the AML Localised Procedures Guideline of their respective 
jurisdiction to obtain more information on adopted AML 
procedures.
8.9 Minimum CDD Measures
The minimum CDD measures should involve:
a) Verifying the customer’s identity using reliable, independent 
source documents, data, or information;
I. In respect of individuals:
i. Full name, DOB, nationality, residential address
ii. Passport, residence visa and others (if applicable)
II. In respect of entities:
i. Company number (copies of official registration documents 
and/or trade licence)
ii. Registered address (physical address rather than PO Box) 
and tax registration number (if applicable)
iii. Unofficial signs of incorporation (letter heads, office 
location, business cards, website, supplier information as 
part of the RPF/quoting process etc.)
iv. Identifying the ultimate beneficial ownership and control 
of the customer and taking reasonable measures to verify 
the identity of the ultimate beneficial owners and controllers 
(UBOs) such that the Company is satisfied that it knows who 
the UBOs are and collection of basic identify information 
including:
• Full name, nationality, residential address;
• Passport and/or other ID document;
v. Obtaining information on the nature of the business and 
the purpose and intended nature of the required services / 
the relationship to be established; and
b) Keeping the above information up to date, and monitoring 
the activity and transactions undertaken by the customer 
throughout the course of the relationship to ensure that it is 
consistent with the Company’s knowledge of the customer.
8.10 Politically Exposed Persons
Politically exposed persons (PEPs) as defined in local 
regulations.
The MLRO shall provide all assistance in case there is any 
uncertainty in identifying such persons, or in answering any 
general questions in this context.
8.11 The Company will obtain internal management 
approval before a Regulated Entity enters into a professional 
relationship with any prospective customer who is a PEP. 
Internal management the CEO’s direct reports who are 
people managers. Such approval may be outsourced where 
applicable in accordance with local laws.

8.13 Source of Funds and wealth 
Source of funds is the activity which generates the funds for 
a customer’s occupation or business activities. Information 
concerning the geographical location of the activities may also 
be relevant.
Source of wealth is distinct from source of funds and describes 
the activities which have generated the total net worth of a 
person both within and outside of the customer relationship, 
i.e. those activities which have generated a customer’s funds 
and property. Information concerning the geographical location 
of the activities that have generated a customer’s wealth 
may also be relevant. In determining source of wealth, it will 
often not be necessary to establish the monetary value of an 
individual’s net worth.
The Company shall demonstrate that it has collected relevant 
relationship information by taking reasonable measures to 
establish source of funds, and where required, take reasonable 
measures to establish source of wealth, for each customer and, 
when third party funding is involved, making further enquiries 
about the relationship between the person providing the funds 
and the customer.
The information collected shall be detailed in a form based on 
the template provided in Annex A, which may be adapted as 
necessary to reflect local regulatory requirements.
8.14 External Data Sources 
Appropriate external data sources will include sources such 
as domestic legislation applying UN and EU sanctions and 
measures, and guidance issued by the concerned regulators, 
and may include information and guidelines published by 
governments and law enforcement authorities on terrorists 
(e.g., United States government agencies such as the Federal 
Bureau of Investigation and OFAC), electronic subscription 
databases, the internet, and other media.
External data sources will also include lists maintained by 
Sanctions Authorities and other regulators, including but 
not limited to (i) the Specially Designated Nationals and 
Blocked Persons List, maintained by the Office of Foreign 
Asset Control (OFAC); (ii) the Consolidated List of Persons 
and Entities subject to Financial Sanctions maintained by the 
European Commission; (iii) the Consolidated List of Financial 
Sanctions Targets in the UK maintained by HM Treasury, 
or (iv) any other list of designated or sanctioned persons 
maintained by a Sanctions Authority

09. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD)
9.1 EDD is performed as an additional measure by the 
MLRO and/or Compliance on High-Risk Customers of 
Regulated Entities, in addition to the usual CDD, to know 
more about the customer, the source of funds and to 
confirm that the transactions are within the customer’s 
means. EDD is necessary in order to verify that funds 
are legitimate and not related to any criminal proceeds 
by obtaining authentic and genuine documents, which 
support both the underlying and stated purpose.
9.2 Additional information to be requested and procedures 
to be performed shall include one or more of the following, 
as applicable to the type of customer (corporate, 
individuals, etc.):
a. Obtain and verify additional customer identification 
document (including of UBOs);
b. Review publicly available information from law 
enforcement agencies or regulatory authorities to 
determine whether customer has been the subject of any 
criminal or civil enforcement action based on violations of 
anti-Money Laundering laws, Sanctions or regulations or 
any criminal investigation, indictment, conviction, or civil 
enforcement action relating to financing of terrorists;
c. Verify that the customer is active and no legal action has 
been taken to dissolve, wind-up or terminate it;
d. Public search (such as Google) for the customer and 
its Directors/Principals/Partners for adverse media 
information and document results;
e. Obtain Bank reference letter/Latest three months bank 
statement;
f. Obtain Credit Report from a reputed lawyer or bank (or 
credit rating report, if any);
g. Assess the customer’s business reputation through 
review of financial or professional references, or by other 
means;
h. Review recent changes in the ownership or senior 
management of the customer;
i. Make a visit to the customer’s place of business and 
conduct a face-to-face meeting with customer or legal 
representative; and
j. If applicable, determine the relationship between the 
customer and the government of its home country 
jurisdiction, including whether the customer is a government-
owned Company.
k. In the case of a PEP, ascertain whether:
• the client is buying a property in his/her own jurisdiction
• the funds for purchase are coming from a bank/
institution regulated in the PEP’s home country.
• Where a PEP is buying in a jurisdiction other than his/her 
own country then the funds to pay us must come from a 
bank/institution regulated in the country of purchase.
10. Non-Compliance
10.1 Where the Company is unable to conduct or complete 
the requisite CDD or EDD in accordance with this AML Policy 
or other legislation, or there are a significant number of 
material unexplained/unmitigated red flags (as set out in 
section 13) were identified, the Company must, to the extent 
relevant (and subject to the advice of the MLRO and Legal):
a. not enter into business relationship with the customer or 
provide services;
b. terminate or suspend any existing business relationship 
with the customer;
c. consider returning any monies (or other property) received 
from the customer; and
d. consider whether the inability to conduct or complete CDD 
/ EDD necessitates the making of a SAR.
10.2 However, the Company must give consideration to the 
risks of ‘tipping off’ the customer or committing Money 
Laundering offences itself (e.g. by returning monies). 
Guidance should be sought from the MLRO and Legal.
10.3 Dar Global accepts payment in cash/credit card per 
unit up to the limits and as per the guidelines provided for 
by local applicable laws. Please refer to the AML Localised 
Procedures Guideline for your Company for applicable limits 
and guidelines.
10.4 Dar Global does not accept direct settlement using 
virtual assets (including cryptocurrencies), however, Dar 
Global will accept payments converted to contract currency 
in local fiat by a locally regulated entities.

11. Sanctions Screening
11.1 The Company shall ensure that it screens its 
recurring customers on an ongoing basis against all 
applicable sanctions lists issued by the relevant Sanctions 
Authorities. The Company will use technology-based 
applications for customer screening.
11.2 To ensure compliance with the relevant sanctions 
against persons and entities, the Company screens the 
names of its prospective customers and customers 
against all relevant Sanctions lists and regulatory 
enforcement lists maintained by the Sanctions Authorities 
through a reputable data amalgamation and search service 
provider.
11.3 Such screening will be conducted prior to any new 
customer being engaged, and on a regular basis thereafter 
while the Company remains in a commercial relationship 
with the customer in question.
12. Transaction Monitoring
12.1 The Company ensures that ongoing transaction 
monitoring is conducted to detect transactions which are 
unusual or potentially suspicious based on the customer 
profile/ behaviour. Any unusual behaviour/ transactions 
shall be escalated through internal channels.
12.2 This process is supplemented by an extensive review 
of the transactions including increased monitoring of the 
customer’s transactions and behaviour.
12.3 The Company does not accept large cash payments 
as per limits established in the AML Localised Procedures 
Guideline.
13. Red Flags
13.1 All the Employees of the Company should be alert 
and vigilant for signs of suspicious activity or behaviour 
that suggests financial crime. Examples of ‘red flags’ that 
Employees may encounter include: 
a. A person refuses, is reluctant to, is unable to, unnecessarily 
delays, or exhibits unusual concern about providing the KYC/
CDD/EDD information;
b. The person appears to be acting as an agent for an 
undisclosed principal, but declines or is reluctant, without 
legitimate commercial reasons, to provide information or is 
otherwise evasive regarding the person or Company;
c. All interactions with the person are conducted remotely 
such that there is no face-to-face interaction, unless 
conducted though portals subject to regulation that ensures 
the person consents to such interaction in the eyes of the 
local law;
d. The person (or a person publicly associated with that 
person) is the subject of news reports indicating possible 
criminal, civil, or regulatory violations;
e. Information provided by a person is false, misleading or 
substantially incorrect or is inconsistent with information 
previously provided;
f. The person insists on dealing only in cash, or asks for 
exemptions from this AML Policy relating to cash payments;
g. The person uses an alternative remittance transfer system 
that does not involve the transfer or intermediation of funds 
through the banking system;
h. Evidence bringing into question the honesty, integrity, 
identity or location of customers;
i. Overpayments or duplicate payments for no apparent 
reason;
j. Significant changes in the size, nature, frequency of 
transactions with a customer that is without reasonable 
explanation; and
k. Cancellation, reversal or requests for refunds of earlier 
transactions without clear reasons, and in particular where 
payments were made ahead of the standard schedule for 
other similar units in the same project. 
13.2 In cases where suspicious transactions and / or 
suspicious behaviour is identified, the MLRO must 
be informed and will, if necessary, conduct further 
investigations.

14. Staff Training
14.1 One of the most important methods the Company has to 
prevent and detect Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing is 
to have staff who are: 
i. alert to Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing risks; and
ii. well trained in the identification of unusual or higher risk 
activities or transactions, that may indicate Money Laundering 
or Terrorist Financing activity. 
14.2 The Company should ensure that the following persons in 
higher risk roles are given appropriate AML training:
a. all commission earners / property consultants;
b. those who handle or are responsible for the handling of

c. those who deal with or manage the customer relationship.
The above employees must attend the AML/CFT training within

15. Record Keeping & Confidentiality
15.1 Dar Global will maintain proof of identity / verification 
records for the minimum period(s) required by the 
applicable laws to align with applicable statutory limitations 
(please verify local requirements in particular for sanctioned 
parties). Departments conducting CDD/EDD must maintain 
all records regarding customers and/or third parties. Finance 
must maintain details of financial transactions carried out.

together with its procedures and controls on an on-going

Policy are based on relevant laws and guidance, as well as a 
risk analysis. If these change materially, the AML Policy will 
be updated. Otherwise, and in all cases, the AML Policy will be

02. Purpose
2.1 This AML Policy sets out the Company’s approach to 
preventing Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing 
by meeting the relevant standards on combatting Money 
Laundering and Terrorism Financing. 
2.2 This AML Policy takes into consideration the following 
pillars of an effective AML program to ensure compliance 
of all its Regulated Entities (as defined below): 
a) Compliance with applicable laws and industry guidance;
b) Identifying Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing 
risks and performing risk assessments;
c) Establishing and maintaining risk-based customer due 
diligence (CDD);
d) Establishing enhanced due diligence (EDD) for 
customers presenting a higher risk;
e) Appointment by each Regulated Entity of a money 
laundering reporting officer and their deputies where 
needed, hereinafter referred to as “MLRO” and entrusting 
roles and responsibilities to combat instances of Money 
Laundering. Regulated Entity means a Company which is 
required by local AML regulations to be registered before 
an AML local authority;
f) Establishing and maintaining risk-based systems and 
procedures for the ongoing monitoring of transactions, 
customers and activities of the Company;
g) Establishing procedures for reporting suspicious activity 
internally and, if necessary, escalation to the relevant law 
enforcement authorities;
h) Localisation of procedures to adhere to local laws;
i) Maintaining appropriate records; and
j) Providing adequate AML training to staff.
03. Scope
3.1 This AML Policy applies to: 
a) Dar Global PLC (Dar Global or we or us) and its 
subsidiaries and any future overseas subsidiaries from 
time to time and ultimately form part of the overall 
ownership/consolidation of a Dar Global (each a Group 
Company or the Company, and collectively referred to as 
the Dar Global Group), and;
b) all directors, officers, and employees, including all 
consultants, agents, brokers, contractors, seconded staff 
and casual workers wherever
3.2 All Employees of the Company shall familiarise 
themselves with the provisions of this AML Policy and 
implementing controls, and the following departments 
play a key role in ensuring compliance with this AML Policy: 
Finance & Accounts, Legal, Compliance, Procurement and 
Sales & Business Development.
3.3 The Company will take reasonable steps to require 
its counterparties to comply with this AML Policy or 
equivalent standards.
3.4 The procedures established in this AML Policy will be 
localised by the Head of Compliance with the support of 
the MLRO to comply with local minimum requirements 
as determined by applicable law and regulations in each 
jurisdiction where the Company operates (AML Localised 
Procedures Guideline).

04. Money Laundering
4.1 The definitions of money laundering and terrorist 
financing differ in different jurisdictions, but in broad 
terms money laundering refers to the acquisition, dealing 
with, or agreement to deal with (or involvement in any 
transaction which facilitates the receipt of or dealing with) 
the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering). Proceeds 
of Crime include all property (including money) that 
you know or suspect is or represents (fully or partially) 
a benefit (direct or indirectly) from criminal conduct. 
Terrorist financing involves the solicitation, collection or 
provision of funds with the intention that they may be 
used to support terrorist acts or organizations (Terrorist 
Financing).
4.2 This AML Policy prohibits all Money Laundering and 
Terrorist Financing. The consequences of non-compliance 
with this AML Policy and relevant applicable laws may 
include imprisonment, fines and/or loss of employment as 
listed below:
4.3 For the Company:
a. criminal liabilities including unlimited fines;
b. confiscation orders;
c. serious reputational damage including media comment; 
d. unenforceability of contracts entered into due to 
illegality
4.4 For Employees:
a. personal criminal liability including fines and/or 
imprisonment;
b. confiscation orders;
c. disciplinary action initiated by the Company, including 
summary dismissal;
d. personal reputational damage; and
e. deportation, where applicable.
05. Regulatory Framework
5.1 The Company is committed to following international 
best practice, including UK regulations where applicable, 
such as the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA), 
international best practices in Anti-Money Laundering 
(AML) & Counter Terrorist Financing (CTF) and the 
Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 (SAMLA), 
Export Control Order 2008 , Counter-Terrorism Act 
2008, Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001 and 
the regulations, licences and guidance that relate to this 
legislation.
5.2 The regulators and government entities that enforce 
these laws expect companies to put in place risk-
based policies and procedures aimed at identifying 
risks of breaching AML and CTF laws and regulations 
and economic, financial or trade sanctions laws, 
export controls, regulations, directives, embargos, 
rules, mandatory guidelines, executive orders or similar 
restrictive measures (Sanctions).
5.3 Many countries in which the Company and its 
subsidiaries operate have enacted laws relating to Money 
Laundering and Terrorist Financing which the Company 
will follow as prescribed. In the
event of any inconsistency, the highest standard will 
generally apply, but you should speak to the MLRO for 
guidance in the case of uncertainty. These countries may 
also impose autonomous Sanctions that are different to 
those enacted and enforced by the Sanctions Authorities, 
and the Company will comply with those Sanctions where 
required.
