06. Money Laundering Reporting 
Officer & Suspicious Activity Report
6.1 Dar Global shall designate a MLRO for each Regulated 
Entity who has the responsibility of ensuring compliance 
with this AML Policy and implementing adequate 
procedures.
6.2 The Group Head of Compliance will be the MLRO’s 
point of contact for any support in fulfilling their 
responsibilities. MLROs and the Head of Compliance will 
have access to legal counsel from the Legal Department 
which shall in turn obtain external counsel if it deems 
necessary..
6.3 The MLRO will act in confidence as a point of 
escalation, provide guidance and clarifications regarding 
this AML Policy, and respond to any questions or enquiries
6.4 If the MLRO receives an internal suspicious activity 
report from an internal department (as per the form set 
out in Appendix D), he/she must, without delay:
a) investigate the circumstances in relation to which the 
report was made; and
b) determine, with the assistance of the legal function 
if the MLRO deems necessary, whether a corresponding 
external suspicious activity report (SAR) should be made 
to the external authorities and if required, make such an 
external report.
6.5 Responsibilities:
The MLRO’s responsibilities include, among others: 
a) Establishing and maintaining effective anti-Money 
Laundering policies, procedures, systems, and controls 
in compliance with applicable legislation according to 
jurisdictional nexus;
b) Assisting employees in their responsibility for complying 
with all relevant regulations, including the provision of 
advice on compliance issues, and acting as the point of 
contact to receive internal suspicious activity reports;
c) Handling any internal suspicious activity reports and taking 
appropriate actions following the receipt of such reports, 
including submitting external SARs to authorities, if required 
by relevant laws;
d) Reporting to Compliance on all relevant material or 
significant breaches and acting as the respective Regulated 
Entity’s point of contact for all external authorities regarding 
Money Laundering issues;
e) Responding promptly to any requests for information 
in relation to Money Laundering issues made by the local 
competent authorities;
f) Maintaining records of due process in line with the relevant 
local laws and this policy in order to respond to any requests 
for information from external authorities regarding Money 
Laundering issues]
g) Supporting and maintaining appropriate anti Money 
Laundering training programs and awareness arrangements; 
and
h) Oversight of know your client (KYC) procedure (as set out 
below).
6.6 Periodic Report
Unless required otherwise under Applicable Law, or triggered 
due to an event that requires immediate attention and 
rectification, the MLRO shall report to senior management on 
an annual basis the MLRO’s proposals for updates required 
to strengthen the Company’s AML compliance framework. 
The report shall also cover any significant breaches and 
other high-risk areas which require management attention. 
The MLRO will send a copy of the report to the relevant 
supervisory authority as required by applicable law.
6.7 Regulatory Co-operation
The MLRO/Head of Compliance shall be the point of contact 
in the Company as regards any communication with 
regulators and therefore, any correspondence received from 
regulators in respect of AML should be promptly forwarded to 
the MLRO/Head of Compliance.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 5

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
7. Risk Based Approach (RBA)
7.1 Customer Risk Assessments
Customer Risk Assessments must be conducted for 
all transactions involving a Regulated Entity. While it is 
essential that the Company complies with the legal and 
regulatory requirements placed upon it, the Company is 
permitted to adopt a risk-based approach in relation to 
Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing. This enables 
the Company to focus its efforts and resources on those 
situations that are of higher risk.
The factors that should be taken into account when 
considering the level of risk that a customer poses include, 
where a risk of Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing or 
Sanctions arise:
a) the jurisdiction in which the customer is registered / 
country of citizenship;
b) the country from which the customer operates;
c) the countries and geographical areas in which the 
customer does business;
d) the nature of the customer’s business and profile of its 
customers;
e) the source of funds of the customer;
f) whether or not, the customer (or a party to the 
transaction) falls within the legal definition of Politically 
Exposed Persons (PEPs).
For transactions with a Regulated Entity, be it the sales 
office or property location, the Sales Administration 
function shall, as part of the CDD process, obtain client 
KYC files and prepare a Client Risk Assessment Report as 
enclosed in Appendix C. For any clients that are rated high 
risk, the file will be submitted to the MLRO and Compliance 
department to conduct an EDD prior to clearance.
7.2 Customer or Counterparty Risk scoring
Guidance for CDD risk rating of customer risk 
subcategories, including geographical and business profiles 
is outlined below.
a) Low Risk:
Low risk customers are those individuals and entities 
whose identity and source of funds can be easily 
determined and whose account transactions by and large 
conform to their known profile. They may include the 
following (subject to a risk assessment):
i. Salaried employees (unless falling within one of the medium 
or high-risk categories below);
ii. Persons / entities registered in known ‘low risk’ jurisdictions;
iii. Persons / entities engaged in industry segments that do not 
make use of complex financial structures;
iv. Government departments/ government owned companies; 
regulators and statutory bodies etc. in low-risk jurisdictions;
v. Regulated banks, financial institutions, credit institutions, 
financial service providers, brokers that are regulated or listed 
or both; and
vi. Publicly listed entities in a low-risk jurisdiction which are 
subject to regulatory supervision.
b) Medium Risk:
Medium risk customers are categorized on the basis of 
their background, nature and location of activity, country of 
residence, sources of funds and customer profile. This could 
include (subject to a risk assessment):
i. High net worth individuals with known sources of income;
ii. PEPs, if acting as only a ‘sponsor’ of the Company;
iii. Persons / entities registered in known ‘medium risk’ 
jurisdictions
iv. Companies having closed family shareholding or beneficial 
ownership; and
v. Entities with silent partners who can be identified.
c) High Risk:
High risk customers typically include persons or corporate 
or associations or beneficial owners residing in high-risk 
countries as identified by any of the international bodies. This 
could include (subject to a risk assessment):
i. PEPs, if not acting as a ‘sponsor’ of the Company;
ii. Non-face to face customers or legal representative;
iii. Entities registered in or conducting business with high-risk 
jurisdictions;
iv. Persons with citizenship/residence in high-risk jurisdictions;
v. Persons / entities engaged in industry segments that are 
complex and/or particularly susceptible to AML risks;
vi. Persons with questionable reputation based on genuine 
-publicly available information;
vii. Trusts, charitable organizations, Non-government 
Organizations (NGOs); and
viii. Organizations receiving donations.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 6

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
7.3 Business Risk Assessment
An effective and documented risk-based approach will enable 
the Company to justify its position on managing Money 
Laundering and terrorist risks to law enforcement, the courts, 
regulators, and supervisory bodies. The Company shall: 
a) Conduct on an annual basis a business risk assessment 
that considers its activities and structure and concludes on 
the Company’s exposure to Money Laundering and Terrorist 
Financing risk. In particular, the Company should consider its 
exposure to risks in relation to its customers, the jurisdictions 
in which it operates and its business.
b) Use the outcome of its business risk assessment to develop 
appropriate risk management systems and controls, and 
necessary updates to its policies and procedures.
7.4 Corporate customer related risks
The business risk assessment will include consideration of 
whether the corporate client:
a) acts for PEPs, particularly those located in jurisdictions with 
high levels of corruption;
b) acts for customers without meeting them i.e., non-face to 
face business
c) practices in locations with high levels of acquisitive crime, or 
for customers who have convictions for acquisitive crimes;
d) acts for customers affiliated to countries with high levels of 
corruption or organized crime, or where terrorist organizations 
operate, or countries with inadequate frameworks to prevent 
and detect Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing;
e) acts for entities that have complex ownership structures; 
and
f) acts for customers for which it cannot obtain details of the 
beneficial owners.
7.5 Real Estate and other Service Risk
The Company’s business risk assessment shall also consider 
different types of risk to which it might be exposed in relation 
to Money Laundering based on real estate structures including 
but not limited to:
a) the handling of cash or assets or through payments that 
are made to, or received from, unregulated third parties, 
particularly with a cross-border element;
b) use of corporate vehicles;
c) use of monetary instruments (including bearer negotiable 
instruments);
d) use of properties to conceal money generated by illegal 
activities; and
e) trusts or other structures that conceal the identities of the 
UBOs 
08. Customer Due Diligence (CDD)
8.1 Regulated Entities follow a KYC process to perform 
identity verification of all customers in accordance with 
applicable AML/CTF regulations, irrespective of the value of 
the transaction.
8.2 Regulated Entities will also ensure the legitimacy of the 
source of funds and the purpose of the transaction.
8.3 Regulated Entities shall maintain proof of identity / 
verification records, watch list and reputational risk search 
results for a minimum period of ten (10) years from the date 
the Regulated Entities ceases to have a relationship with the 
customer.
8.4 Customers are required to provide information in 
the Client Registration Form to their contact in the Sales 
Administration department prior to entering into any 
transactions with the Regulated Entities. The information 
collected shall be detailed in a form form based on the 
templates provided in this AML Policy Appendix – A (for 
individuals) and Appendix – B (for corporate entities), which 
may be adapted as necessary to reflect local regulatory 
requirements,.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 7

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
8.5 Sanctions Screening  
The Company is committed to adhering to all relevant 
Sanctions adopted, administered or enforced by relevant 
sanctions authorities which may include (without limitation) 
those sanctions regimes administered and enforced by 
authorities including the United Kingdom, the U.S. Government 
(including, without limitation, the U.S. Department of the 
Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the U.S. 
Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Commerce), 
the European Union, or the Security Council of the United 
Nations (each of the foregoing, together with any other relevant 
regulatory authority, being a Sanctions Authority).
8.6 The Company is committed to ensuring that it does not, 
knowingly, do business with anyone whose name either 
appears on a Sanctions list (see 11 below). Clients who are from 
a country listed on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) list of 
Non-Cooperative Countries & Territories (NCCT), or any other 
country-specific list where the customer is operating shall 
have the highest risk rating for the geographic risk in the CDD 
assessment.
8.7 The Company will screen all prospective customers and 
customers in accordance with 11.3 below. Any commercial 
relationships or transactions that appear to involve (directly or 
indirectly) countries, entities, or individuals that are targeted by 
Sanctions must be brought to the attention of the MLRO before 
any action is taken.
8.8 Companies which are not Regulated Entities shall refer to 
the AML Localised Procedures Guideline of their respective 
jurisdiction to obtain more information on adopted AML 
procedures.
8.9 Minimum CDD Measures
The minimum CDD measures should involve:
a) Verifying the customer’s identity using reliable, independent 
source documents, data, or information;
I. In respect of individuals:
i. Full name, DOB, nationality, residential address
ii. Passport, residence visa and others (if applicable)
II. In respect of entities:
i. Company number (copies of official registration documents 
and/or trade licence)
ii. Registered address (physical address rather than PO Box) 
and tax registration number (if applicable)
iii. Unofficial signs of incorporation (letter heads, office 
location, business cards, website, supplier information as 
part of the RPF/quoting process etc.)
iv. Identifying the ultimate beneficial ownership and control 
of the customer and taking reasonable measures to verify 
the identity of the ultimate beneficial owners and controllers 
(UBOs) such that the Company is satisfied that it knows who 
the UBOs are and collection of basic identify information 
including:
• Full name, nationality, residential address;
• Passport and/or other ID document;
v. Obtaining information on the nature of the business and 
the purpose and intended nature of the required services / 
the relationship to be established; and
b) Keeping the above information up to date, and monitoring 
the activity and transactions undertaken by the customer 
throughout the course of the relationship to ensure that it is 
consistent with the Company’s knowledge of the customer.
8.10 Politically Exposed Persons
Politically exposed persons (PEPs) as defined in local 
regulations.
The MLRO shall provide all assistance in case there is any 
uncertainty in identifying such persons, or in answering any 
general questions in this context.
8.11 The Company will obtain internal management 
approval before a Regulated Entity enters into a professional 
relationship with any prospective customer who is a PEP. 
Internal management the CEO’s direct reports who are 
people managers. Such approval may be outsourced where 
applicable in accordance with local laws.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 8

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03

Determination and Recording of Risk for Regulated Entities
The information set out at section 8.9 must be collected to enable a customer profile to be 
prepared.
Evaluate the information collected in Stage 1 and appropriate external data sources and 
consider whether it is appropriate to collect further information.
Determine and record an initial risk assessment for the customer and determine the client’s 
risk category, as set out in section 7.2 above and the corresponding level of CDD / EDD. Where a 
customer is designated as High Risk, EDD will be required. 
Application of a Risk Based Approach
The Company must periodically update relevant CDD information and its risk assessment (in 
line with Stages 1 to 3). In the event where the Company is officially notified of any change in 
beneficial ownership or control of the customer, or third parties on whose behalf the customer 
acts, reasonable measures should be taken to verify the identity.
Frequency of CDD update & risk assessment for recurring customers shall be decided based on 
the risk categorization as follows:
1. Low-Risk customers: Once in three years (updated License/KYC documents will be 
obtained)
2. Medium-Risk customers: Once in two years (updated License/KYC documents will be 
obtained)
3. High-Risk / EDD customers: Updated License/KYC documents will be obtained every time a 
new service is requested irrespective of the time period along with an annual assessment 
for all such customers 
Note: Irrespective of the time specified above, CDD shall be refreshed when material changes 
or events occur relating to a customer.
8.12 Risk-based approach to CDD 
As set out in section 7, a risk-based approach to CDD should be undertaken.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
8.13 Source of Funds and wealth 
Source of funds is the activity which generates the funds for 
a customer’s occupation or business activities. Information 
concerning the geographical location of the activities may also 
be relevant.
Source of wealth is distinct from source of funds and describes 
the activities which have generated the total net worth of a 
person both within and outside of the customer relationship, 
i.e. those activities which have generated a customer’s funds 
and property. Information concerning the geographical location 
of the activities that have generated a customer’s wealth 
may also be relevant. In determining source of wealth, it will 
often not be necessary to establish the monetary value of an 
individual’s net worth.
The Company shall demonstrate that it has collected relevant 
relationship information by taking reasonable measures to 
establish source of funds, and where required, take reasonable 
measures to establish source of wealth, for each customer and, 
when third party funding is involved, making further enquiries 
about the relationship between the person providing the funds 
and the customer.
The information collected shall be detailed in a form based on 
the template provided in Annex A, which may be adapted as 
necessary to reflect local regulatory requirements.
8.14 External Data Sources 
Appropriate external data sources will include sources such 
as domestic legislation applying UN and EU sanctions and 
measures, and guidance issued by the concerned regulators, 
and may include information and guidelines published by 
governments and law enforcement authorities on terrorists 
(e.g., United States government agencies such as the Federal 
Bureau of Investigation and OFAC), electronic subscription 
databases, the internet, and other media.
External data sources will also include lists maintained by 
Sanctions Authorities and other regulators, including but 
not limited to (i) the Specially Designated Nationals and 
Blocked Persons List, maintained by the Office of Foreign 
Asset Control (OFAC); (ii) the Consolidated List of Persons 
and Entities subject to Financial Sanctions maintained by the 
European Commission; (iii) the Consolidated List of Financial 
Sanctions Targets in the UK maintained by HM Treasury, 
or (iv) any other list of designated or sanctioned persons 
maintained by a Sanctions Authority
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 10

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
09. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD)
9.1 EDD is performed as an additional measure by the 
MLRO and/or Compliance on High-Risk Customers of 
Regulated Entities, in addition to the usual CDD, to know 
more about the customer, the source of funds and to 
confirm that the transactions are within the customer’s 
means. EDD is necessary in order to verify that funds 
are legitimate and not related to any criminal proceeds 
by obtaining authentic and genuine documents, which 
support both the underlying and stated purpose.
9.2 Additional information to be requested and procedures 
to be performed shall include one or more of the following, 
as applicable to the type of customer (corporate, 
individuals, etc.):
a. Obtain and verify additional customer identification 
document (including of UBOs);
b. Review publicly available information from law 
enforcement agencies or regulatory authorities to 
determine whether customer has been the subject of any 
criminal or civil enforcement action based on violations of 
anti-Money Laundering laws, Sanctions or regulations or 
any criminal investigation, indictment, conviction, or civil 
enforcement action relating to financing of terrorists;
c. Verify that the customer is active and no legal action has 
been taken to dissolve, wind-up or terminate it;
d. Public search (such as Google) for the customer and 
its Directors/Principals/Partners for adverse media 
information and document results;
e. Obtain Bank reference letter/Latest three months bank 
statement;
f. Obtain Credit Report from a reputed lawyer or bank (or 
credit rating report, if any);
g. Assess the customer’s business reputation through 
review of financial or professional references, or by other 
means;
h. Review recent changes in the ownership or senior 
management of the customer;
i. Make a visit to the customer’s place of business and 
conduct a face-to-face meeting with customer or legal 
representative; and
j. If applicable, determine the relationship between the 
customer and the government of its home country 
jurisdiction, including whether the customer is a government-
owned Company.
k. In the case of a PEP, ascertain whether:
• the client is buying a property in his/her own jurisdiction
• the funds for purchase are coming from a bank/
institution regulated in the PEP’s home country.
• Where a PEP is buying in a jurisdiction other than his/her 
own country then the funds to pay us must come from a 
bank/institution regulated in the country of purchase.
10. Non-Compliance
10.1 Where the Company is unable to conduct or complete 
the requisite CDD or EDD in accordance with this AML Policy 
or other legislation, or there are a significant number of 
material unexplained/unmitigated red flags (as set out in 
section 13) were identified, the Company must, to the extent 
relevant (and subject to the advice of the MLRO and Legal):
a. not enter into business relationship with the customer or 
provide services;
b. terminate or suspend any existing business relationship 
with the customer;
c. consider returning any monies (or other property) received 
from the customer; and
d. consider whether the inability to conduct or complete CDD 
/ EDD necessitates the making of a SAR.
10.2 However, the Company must give consideration to the 
risks of ‘tipping off’ the customer or committing Money 
Laundering offences itself (e.g. by returning monies). 
Guidance should be sought from the MLRO and Legal.
10.3 Dar Global accepts payment in cash/credit card per 
unit up to the limits and as per the guidelines provided for 
by local applicable laws. Please refer to the AML Localised 
Procedures Guideline for your Company for applicable limits 
and guidelines.
10.4 Dar Global does not accept direct settlement using 
virtual assets (including cryptocurrencies), however, Dar 
Global will accept payments converted to contract currency 
in local fiat by a locally regulated entities.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 11

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
11. Sanctions Screening
11.1 The Company shall ensure that it screens its 
recurring customers on an ongoing basis against all 
applicable sanctions lists issued by the relevant Sanctions 
Authorities. The Company will use technology-based 
applications for customer screening.
11.2 To ensure compliance with the relevant sanctions 
against persons and entities, the Company screens the 
names of its prospective customers and customers 
against all relevant Sanctions lists and regulatory 
enforcement lists maintained by the Sanctions Authorities 
through a reputable data amalgamation and search service 
provider.
11.3 Such screening will be conducted prior to any new 
customer being engaged, and on a regular basis thereafter 
while the Company remains in a commercial relationship 
with the customer in question.
12. Transaction Monitoring
12.1 The Company ensures that ongoing transaction 
monitoring is conducted to detect transactions which are 
unusual or potentially suspicious based on the customer 
profile/ behaviour. Any unusual behaviour/ transactions 
shall be escalated through internal channels.
12.2 This process is supplemented by an extensive review 
of the transactions including increased monitoring of the 
customer’s transactions and behaviour.
12.3 The Company does not accept large cash payments 
as per limits established in the AML Localised Procedures 
Guideline.
13. Red Flags
13.1 All the Employees of the Company should be alert 
and vigilant for signs of suspicious activity or behaviour 
that suggests financial crime. Examples of ‘red flags’ that 
Employees may encounter include: 
a. A person refuses, is reluctant to, is unable to, unnecessarily 
delays, or exhibits unusual concern about providing the KYC/
CDD/EDD information;
b. The person appears to be acting as an agent for an 
undisclosed principal, but declines or is reluctant, without 
legitimate commercial reasons, to provide information or is 
otherwise evasive regarding the person or Company;
c. All interactions with the person are conducted remotely 
such that there is no face-to-face interaction, unless 
conducted though portals subject to regulation that ensures 
the person consents to such interaction in the eyes of the 
local law;
d. The person (or a person publicly associated with that 
person) is the subject of news reports indicating possible 
criminal, civil, or regulatory violations;
e. Information provided by a person is false, misleading or 
substantially incorrect or is inconsistent with information 
previously provided;
f. The person insists on dealing only in cash, or asks for 
exemptions from this AML Policy relating to cash payments;
g. The person uses an alternative remittance transfer system 
that does not involve the transfer or intermediation of funds 
through the banking system;
h. Evidence bringing into question the honesty, integrity, 
identity or location of customers;
i. Overpayments or duplicate payments for no apparent 
reason;
j. Significant changes in the size, nature, frequency of 
transactions with a customer that is without reasonable 
explanation; and
k. Cancellation, reversal or requests for refunds of earlier 
transactions without clear reasons, and in particular where 
payments were made ahead of the standard schedule for 
other similar units in the same project. 
13.2 In cases where suspicious transactions and / or 
suspicious behaviour is identified, the MLRO must 
be informed and will, if necessary, conduct further 
investigations.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY
Page 12

ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY, 2025 24 SEPTEMBER, 2025V.03
14. Staff Training
14.1 One of the most important methods the Company has to 
prevent and detect Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing is 
to have staff who are: 
i. alert to Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing risks; and
ii. well trained in the identification of unusual or higher risk 
activities or transactions, that may indicate Money Laundering 
or Terrorist Financing activity. 
14.2 The Company should ensure that the following persons in 
higher risk roles are given appropriate AML training:
a. all commission earners / property consultants;
b. those who handle or are responsible for the handling of 
customer services; and
c. those who deal with or manage the customer relationship.
The above employees must attend the AML/CFT training within 
three months of joining and at least on an annual basis. 
15. Record Keeping & Confidentiality
15.1 Dar Global will maintain proof of identity / verification 
records for the minimum period(s) required by the 
applicable laws to align with applicable statutory limitations 
(please verify local requirements in particular for sanctioned 
parties). Departments conducting CDD/EDD must maintain 
all records regarding customers and/or third parties. Finance 
must maintain details of financial transactions carried out.
ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING POLICY

Dar Global PLC 
Anti-Bribery & Corruption Policy

ANTI-BRIBERY AND CORRUPTION POLICY – v2 SEP 2024

1. Introduction 
1.1 Dar Global PLC (“Dar Global” or "the Company" or “we” or “us”  or “the group” ) is committed to a culture of good 
business ethics and integrity and has zero tolerance of all forms of Bribery and Corruption (as defined in 4.4 below). 
The Company has a zero -tolerance approach to any of its directors, officers , employees or third parties ( in their 
relationship with the Company), being involved in Bribery or Corruption, whether by offering, promising, soliciting, 
demanding, giving or accepting a Bribe or behaving corruptly in the expectation of a Bribe or an advantage. The Policy 
is based upon Organization for Economic Co- operation and Development (OECD) Anti-Bribery Convention, United 
Nations Convention against Corruption, United Kingdom Bribery Act 2010, Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and 
other applicable anti-Bribery and Corruption legislation (ABC Laws). 
2. Objectives 
2.1 To set out the Company’s anti-Bribery and Corruption standards and provide its directors, officers, employees  and 
those who act on its behalf with clear requirements and guidelines on the prevention, detection and reporting of 
behavior in compliance with applicable ABC Laws and best practices. 
2.2 To set out the potential consequences of failure to comply with ABC Laws and the Policy. 
2.3 To further elaborate on the anti-Bribery and Corruption principles set out in the Company’s Code of Conduct Policy. 
3. Scope 
3.1 This Policy applies to: 
(a) Dar Global PLC , a company incorporated in England with registered number 14388348 and its subsidiaries  
including any future overseas developments  from time  to time and ultimately form part of  the overall 
ownership/consolidation of the Company (each a “Group Company”, collectively referred to as the “Dar Global 
Group, “Company”, “Group” ), and all directors, officers, and employees, including all consultants, contractors, 
seconded staff and casual workers wherever located (Employees); and 
(b) All of those individuals or companies who provide services to, or act for or on behalf of the Group in any capacity, 
including agents, sponsors, intermediaries, representatives, and introducers (each an Associated Person). 
 
4. Legal overview and definitions 
4.1 The Group always acts responsibly, honestly and with integrity and  has a zero -tolerance policy to any non -
compliance with ABC Laws.  
4.2 Breaches of ABC Laws or this Policy shall not be tolerated and may be considered as gross misconduct , which may 
result in a disciplinary action leading to a summary dismissal without notice and/or other legal actions. 
4.3 This Policy applies to private Bribery (i.e. where none of the persons involved are public officials), as well as Bribes 
involving Public Officials.  
4.4 For the purposes of this Policy: 
 A Bribe is anything of value given , promised, solicited  or offered with the intent to improperly influence the 
recipient or another to act in your or another’s favour , even if  authorized by management. Bribes can be money 
payments – a gift, kickback, excessive commission or other payment –  but nearly anything can be a Bribe. A Bribe 
also includes a Facilitation Payment (as defined in 5.3 below). Examples can include gifts, services, lavish travel and 
hospitality, offers of employment or internships, or any form of preferential treatment.  
 A kickback is where the bribe payer, usually the supplier of goods or services, overcharges a client, paying some or 
all of the overcharge to a representative of the client in return for being awarded a contract or continuing to receive 
business from that client, or some other business advantage. 
 Bribery is offering, promising, authorizing, giving, soliciting, seeking or accepting any financial or other advantage, 
to induce the recipient or any other person to act improperly in the performance of their functions, or to reward 
them for acting improperly, or where the recipient would act improperly by accepting the advantage.  
 Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power or position for private gain.  
 A Public Official shall be broadly interpreted and means: 
i. any elected or appointed Government official (e.g. a legislator or a member of a Government ministry); 
ii. any member of the judiciary or any person who otherwise performs a judicial or quasi-judicial function; 
iii. any employee or individual acting for or on behalf of a Government Official, a State-Owned or State-Controlled 
Enterprises, agency or enterprise performing a governmental function, a public international organization, a 
company owned or controlled in whole or in part by, a Government, (e.g. an entity hired to review bids on 
behalf of a government agency, a public University professor, etc.);

iv. any political party officer, candidate for public office, officer, or employee or individual acting for or on behalf 
of a political party or candidate for public office; 
v. any employee or individual acting for or on behalf of a public international organization (e.g. the World Bank, 
the United Nations, the European Commission);  
vi. any candidates for political offices;  
vii. any member of a royal family or a member of the military; and 
viii. any individual otherwise categorized as a Government Official under applicable law. 
 “Government” means all levels and subdivisions of governments, including local, regional, national, administrative, 
legislative or executive. 
4.5 Under the UK Bribery Act 2010, it is an offence for a corporation carrying on business (or part of a business) in the 
UK to fail to prevent Bribery including but not limited to Bribery by Employees, subsidiaries and Associated Persons. 
This applies to acts committed anywhere in the world which are intended to benefit the corporation .  The only 
defense to an offence of failing to prevent B ribery is that the corporation can demonstrate that it has “ adequate 
procedures” to prevent Bribery. 
4.6 Local laws: Almost all countries in which the Company and its subsidiaries operate have enacted ABC L aws 
criminalizing, at least, the offer of Bribes and kickbacks to Public Officials. Local laws may also impose limits on gifts, 
hospitality, and other promotional expenses. 
4.7 Key Elements: This Policy  is designed to comply with international best practices, building on the following key 
elements that are illustrated hereinafter: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4.8 Consequences of non-Compliance: The consequences of non-compliance with ABC Laws or with this Policy  may 
include imprisonment, financial penalty and/or loss of employment as listed below: 
(a) For the Company: 
• criminal or civil liabilities including unlimited fines and / or disgorgement of profits; 
• serious reputational damage including media comment; 
• debarment from tendering for public sector contracts; and 
• unenforceability of contracts entered into due to acts of Bribery, fraud or other illegality. 
(b) For Employees: 
• personal criminal liability including fines and/or imprisonment; 
• disciplinary action initiated by the Company, including summary dismissal;

(c) For Associated Persons:  
 In addition to the above, any Associated Person found to have violated the Policy or ABC Laws may be subject

4.9 Your responsibilities 
You must: 
• READ and comply with this Policy. 
• Take RESPONSIBILITY for the prevention, detection and reporting of B ribery and Corruption, 
including any activity that might lead to, or suggest, a breach of this Policy. 
• REPORT as soon as possible if you believe or suspect that a breach of this Policy has occurred, or may 
occur in the future. 
 
5. Key Risk Areas and Requirements 
The Group generally prohibits the  Development, Construction and Procurement department  from accepting any Gifts 
(including promotional items) and Hospitality on an individual basis . The Procurement department may only accept to 
attend corporate events with the approval of the Group Head of Procurement where Dar Global is officially engaged as 
an organization, which would involve a group of Dar Global employees.  Other employees may accept gifts provided they 
comply with this policy. 
The Group’s second and third line s of defense (Risk, Compliance and Audit)  are not permitted to accept any g ifts, and 
may only accept nominal levels of Hospitality as described below. 
Gifts and Hospitality received by the CEO  that require manager approval will be subject to approval by the Compliance 
department. 
Below are specific situations identified that may present concern about the potential for B ribery or Corruption. 
Compliance will conduct an annual Bribery and Corruption risk assessment through interviews with key business heads 
and update this list of situations as appropriate. 
 
5.1 Gifts and Hospitality  
Employees or Associated persons acting on behalf of the C ompany may not offer, provide, request or accept Gifts or 
Hospitality from third parties (as defined below)  that could affect the receiving party’s impartiality, or influence or 
induce a business decision, e.g. 
i. Gifts / Hospitality that are excessively lavish or which are conditional on particular behaviours or 
conduct;  
ii. Gifts / Hospitality which are disproportionate to the role and means of the recipient; 
iii. Gifts /Hospitality which are used to obligate, or appear to obligate, the recipient or influence the 
recipient to act or not act in a particular way; 
iv. Gifts / Hospitality which are not provided openly and transparently; or 
v. Gifts / Hospitality whilst they are part of a tendering process directly or indirectly involving the third 
party. 
 
For these purposes:  
(a) a Gift is anything of value offered or given to an individual, a member of their family or business partner, and 
could include, for example: cash or cash equivalent (e.g. vouchers and prepaid cards), gift baskets, tickets to an 
event where the employee and third party do not attend together, travel or accommodation not connected to a 
business event, gift certificates, artwork, jewelry , electronics , offers of employment or internships , use of 
vacation facilities or hotels. 
(b) Hospitality is an event to which you accompany a third party, and could include, for example, a meal, sports 
match, event or concert and any travelling, accommodation and refreshments (if you do not accompany the third 
party, the Hospitality should be treated as a Gift).

Employees must register (see 5.4) and seek written approval for Gifts or Hospitality received or provided as required 
by the guidelines set out below. The conditions for acceptance and approval requirements for providing; and receiving 
Gifts and Hospitality, from business contacts and public officials are set out below.  
 
Employees are strictly prohibited from: 
• Requesting gifts from third parties; 
• Accepting cash or a cash equivalent (such as gift vouchers, certificates with a set negotiable value); 
• Accepting any gift of a value over $50 (although the offer and refusal of that gift should be recorded through 
the gifts register); 
• Giving or receiving any gift other than promotional items, to a public official; 
• Accepting gifts of any kind during a tendering process or in any other circumstances where it could give the 
appearance of being given to influence a business decision;  
• Accepting any gift in circumstances where the receipt would or could appear to be improper.  
 
In order to ensure transparency and oversight, employees must record all offered gifts of a more than nominal value 
(promotional items of less than $15) on our centralized gifts register whether they have been accepted or declined. 
In assessing the value of the gift offered, employees are required to take a sensible approach, which may include an 
internet search if the value is not immediately clear. 
 
Employees should refuse any gift offered which is valued at more than $50. The only exception to this is where the 
gift was intended and is capable of being shared between the team – such as a case of wine or gift basket containing 
multiple items where the division of the gift between team members would result in each team member accepting a 
gift of less than $50. Consent from the line manager must be sought and such a gift recorded on the register. Where 
a gift requires consent from a line manager and/or entry on the gift register, this ought to be done as soon as possible 
and in any event within five working days.  
 
Employees must submit all expense claims relating to gifts provided to third parties in accordance with our expenses 
policy and record the reason for expenditure on the gift register. All accounts, invoices, and other records relating to 
dealings with third parties including suppliers and customers should be prepared with strict accuracy and 
completeness. Accounts must not be kept “off-book” to facilitate or conceal improper payments.

Hospitality may be given or received as part of the development and maintenance of healthy and productive working 
relationships with our clients and partners, however it is important that employees consider the context in which 
hospitality is provided to e nsure that it could not be perceived as an attempt to influence the judgement of the 
recipient improperly, or impact how they perform their functions.  
 
Employees, in deciding whether to give or receive hospitality should consider: 
• How frequently the hospitality has been given or received –  has this client been taken for dinner at a much 
greater frequency than others? 
• Is there an active tender or decision being made which would make the provision or receipt of hospitality 
inappropriate? Could it give the appearance of impropriety?  
• Is the value of the hospitality being offered such that it gives the appearance of impropriety?  
• Has there been any suggestion that the hospitality is kept ‘off the books’? 
 
Employees are strictly prohibited from: 
• Requesting hospitality from third parties; 
• Accepting hospitality provided from a third party whilst they are part of a tendering process  directly or 
indirectly involving the third party; 
• Giving or accepting hospitality which would cause embarrassment to the company by virtue of the activity 
offered or the venue in which it was provided; 
• Giving any hospitality to public officials, or accepting more than nominal hospitality (such as refreshments 
during meetings) from public officials; 
• Accepting or receiving any hospitality which may create an appearance of impropriety.  
 
In order to ensure transparency and oversight, employees must record hospitality in line with the requirements set 
out below on our a uthorizing gifts register. The employee should set out the client, the reason for the hospitality, 
type and value and any material considerations for the supervisor as set out above. 
 
Where employees are required to seek line manager approval, they are required to do so in advance of receiving the 
hospitality, or where this is not possible, within five business days. Dar Global has set a reasonable cap on the giving 
and receiving of hospitality for business development purposes at $200 per person. In extraordinary circumstances, 
where hospitality is likely to exceed $200, employees must seek prior consent from the Group CEO setting out the 
nature, purpose and estimated value of the hospitality. This must be recorded on the hospitality register.   
 
A failure to seek consent and record hospitality where required is a breach of this policy and may result in 
disciplinary action. As such, appropriate planning should be conducted by those involved in engagement with third 
parties such as  Government Relations,  Business Development, Human Resources  and Procurement/Contractor 
management to anticipate and pre-authorise potential hospitality scenarios. 
 
Employees must submit all expenses claims relating to hospitality provided to third parties in accordance with our 
expenses policy and record the reason for expenditure. All accounts, invoices, and other records relating to dealings 
with third parties incl uding suppliers and customers should be prepared with strict accuracy and completeness. 
Accounts must not be kept “off-book” to facilitate or conceal improper payments.

5.2 Expenditures in connection with Public Officials 
The Group generally prohibits its Employees and /  or Associated Persons, either directly or through  a third party, 
from offering, promising,  authorizing or providing a payment or anything of value (including Gifts or Hospitality) to 
a Public Official or to another person at the Public Official ’s request to obtain or retain business or an advantage in 
the conduct of business. 
Under limited circumstances, ABC L aws may allow for appropriate, reasonable, and bona fide expenditure in 
connection with Public Officials. Prior written approval from your Head of the Business Unit and Head of Compliance 
must be secured in advance of offering or incurring any such expenditure.  
 
5.3 Unapproved Gifts 
Unapproved gifts received will be returned to the donor on a best-efforts endeavor. The treatment such gifts received 
that can not be returned to the donor, including due to inability to establish contact after monthly attempts for 90 
days, will be subject to the CEO and Head of Compliance’s decision to donate to charitable causes and in line with the 
charitable donations clauses of Dar Global’s policies. 
 
5.4 Gifts register 
Employees are required to complete any mandatory fields as well as optional fields as appropriate in gifts register. 
Guidelines for information to be captured may be found in the Gift Register Manual, and includes: 
• Type: Gift/Hospitality 
• Date of the gift: This helps to track the timing of the gift and to ensure that it was not given or received in 
connection with any specific business transaction. 
• Name of the giver and affiliation: The name and affiliation of the person or organization providing the 
gift. 
• Name of the recipient and affiliation: The name and affiliation of the individual or department within the 
company receiving the gift. 
• Relationship to Business: Information regarding the business relationship between the giver and the 
recipient, including any ongoing or potential business dealings. 
• Purpose of the gift, context and circumstances: This provides an explanation for why the gift was given 
or received (e.g. celebration, appreciation, or recognition). 
• Estimated value of the gift in USD. 
• Description of the gift: A detailed description of the gift, including its nature, and any relevant 
specifications. 
• Approvals: This field indicates whether the gift was approved by authorized persons. 
• Gift Accepted/Declined. 
• Reason for accepting/declining. 
• Supporting documentation (upload). 
• Manager’s online sign-off: confirming all approvals have been obtained 
• Manager’s comments: relevant observations, if any. 
Employees must always seek approval prior to engaging or providing anything of value to  a Public official 
(excluding DAR branded giveaways)

5.5 Facilitation Payments 
Facilitation Payments include payments made or goods provided to perform, or expedite, a routine duty and or speed 
up the performance of any formal standard procedures irrespective of size or frequency. Examples of actions 
constituting Facilitation Payments include: 
• requests by custom officials for “undue custom duties” for the prompt clearing of items; 
• payments to speed up the process of granting licenses or permits – “special acceleration fees”; and 
• payments to ensure prompt transit of equipment or cargo – “assurance payments”. 
A payment made in accordance with any officially established and legitimate ‘fast track ’ services which may be 
available does not amount to a Facilitation Payment. Such payments must be made directly to the government body 
or private entity and not to an individual person and payments must be properly documented and records 
maintained for a period of no less than ten years. 
The Company, its  Employees and Associated Persons must not make Facilitation Payments even where such 
payments are customary or local practice. The Company accepts that refusal to make illicit payments may lead to 
commercial delays and there may be an immediate commercial cost to the company attributable to this Policy.  
 
5.6 Business Relationships with Associated Persons including Procurement 
The Group expects all Associated Persons to share the Company’s values and ethical standards. The Company may be 
liable under ABC Laws not only for the actions of its Employees but also in certain circumstances for the actions of 
its Associated Persons. 
The Company expects Associated Persons to comply with ABC Laws and this Policy to approach matters of B ribery 
and Corruption in a manner that is consistent with the principles set out in this Policy.  
All Associated Persons must be engaged through a fair, formal procurement process, and in accordance with the Dar 
Global 3rd Party Service Provider Policy . Any procurement and contracting decisions should be based on the best 
value expected to be received, considering the merits of price, quality, performance, time, competency, and  
compliance. 
No Employees may solicit or accept any financial or other advantage as an inducement or reward for the improper 
performance of their duties related to procurement or contracting decisions. 
Business relationships with Associated Persons represent a significant area of risk for the Company. The following 
procedures should be followed and documented accurately  for all Associated Persons prior to entering into any 
relationship with the Associated Person: 
(a) The Company will ensure that the procurement procedures for engaging and appointing third parties are open, 
fair and transparent. 
(b) The Employees shall ensure full compliance with the Procurement Policy, process, and procedures available, 
which shall be periodically monitored by the Compliance department, and to be audited as per the approved 
audit plan frequency by the Internal Audit department. 
(c) The Head of Compliance is responsible for conducting periodic assurance reviews that the Company carries 
out due diligence enquiries in accordance with the Dar Global 3rd Party Service Provider Policy to review the 
integrity records of Associated Persons before entering into a commercial relationship with them. The 
assessment should be risk based and assess the risk of Bribery and Corruption with reference to jurisdiction, 
transaction, business opportunity and relationship. Where there is an identified significant risk of Bribery 
and Corruption, or red flags in the standard due diligence procedure are observed, enhanced due diligence 
should be undertaken. 
(d) The Company should ensure that no Conflict of Interest or perceptions of Conflict of Interest as those terms 
are defined in the HR Handbook (Employee Conflict of Interest section) exist, or if they do exist, that they are 
properly declared, managed or waived.  
(e) The Company should ensure appropriate contractual protections are put in place; document the business 
need and clearly record the decisions made.  
In the event there is deemed to be a significant risk of Bribery or Corruption, all Employees must consult the 
Head of Compliance in relation to appropriate anti-Bribery and Corruption measures before: 
• appointing or offering to appoint a new supplier/subcontractor; 
• entering into or offering a partnership/joint venture arrangement; 
• appointing or offering to appoint an agent to work on behalf of the Company; 
• offering to enter into a new contract or offering to amend the terms of an existing contract; or

• accepting/giving up any mutual claim in a dispute with a third party. 
 
 
5.7 Recruitment of Employees 
The Company will provide an equal opportunity for the employment or appointment of any qualified and competent 
candidate and will not tolerate discrimination in the hiring of suitable candidates. Recruitment must be based on 
approved selection criteria to ensure that only the most qualified and suitable individuals are employed or appointed 
and to ensure that no element of Bribery or Corruption is involved. 
Proper background checks should be conducted by the HR team or third party to ensure that the potential Employee 
has not been convicted of or investigated in relation to any Bribery or Corruption offences anywhere in the world.  
 
5.8 Personal Conflict of Interest 
The Employees of the Company must avoid situations or transactions in which their personal interests could conflict, 
or might appear to be in conflict, with the interests of the Company. 
Conflict of interest can arise if individuals have a personal interest in business dealings involving the C ompany. 
Personal interest can be direct or indirect and refers not only to personal interests but to those of family members 
and friends. If there is a potential for conflict, the interests of the Company must take priority. 
Employees must disclose any personal conflict of interest or potential perceived conflict to their line manager and 
others in accordance with the terms of the Conflicts of Interest and Code of Conduct p olicies; please refer to  both 
these policies for more information. 
 
5.9 Charitable Donations 
As part of its strategy, the Company may provide charitable donations and sponsorship to various organizations and 
institutions in the regions where it conducts its business.  The Company may also support local charities or provide 
sponsorship for cultural events.  
Any such sponsorship should be transparent and properly documented. The Company will only provide donations to 
organizations that serve a legitimate public purpose, and which are themselves subject to high standards of 
transparency and accountability.  
In the implementation of any ESG or corporate social responsibility (CSR) and sponsorship programs, the Company 
and its Employees shall make every effort to provide reasonable assurance that the assistance provided will no t be 
used for corrupt purposes.  
Appropriate due diligence by the Compliance  department, ensuring the charity is properly registered and contact 
information is consistent with registers on government portals, and verifying with Compliance that it is not subject 
to Sanctions; this must be conducted on the proposed recipient charity which shall be pre-approved by CEO. 
The Company does not make any donations to any political party,  government entities, organizations or individuals 
engaged in politics. This includes any monetary donations, donations of goods and/or services, or having Employees 
volunteer on behalf of the Company.  
 
6. Guidance on refusing gifts or entertainment 
Refusing gifts and customary hospitality can be awkward, in circumstances where employees  can not accept gifts/hospitality 
or are unsure whether they  can accept  such gifts/hospitality, employees should politely refuse keeping their hands to 
themselves, and may express such refusal as follows: 
“Thank you very much for your generosity, I hate to refuse this, but it is unfortunately against our company policies and code 
of ethics to accept such gifts/hospitality without first obtaining approval from management.” Continue refusing politely should 
Employees must notify the Company of any personal connection or interest they have in its business dealings 
 
Employees must not make donations on behalf of the Company without prior authorization. 
 
Employees must notify the Company of any personal connection they have with potential Employees.

your counterpart insist. 
If you have reason to believe you could be placed in a position during a planned encounter where such gifts/hospitality  may 
be offered to you, it is good practice to gain pre-approval in writing in line with limits set in this policy. 
 
7. Accounting provisions: accurate books and records 
The Company must make and keep books, records and accounts that accurately and fairly reflect its transactions and 
disposition of assets in sufficient detail to facilitate a full understanding and audit trail, according to the Finance Policy. 
No false or misleading entries should be made and all entries should completely and accurately describe the 
transactions to which they are related. 
No payment on behalf of the Company should be approved without adequate supporting documentation or made with 
the intention or understanding that all or  part of any such payment is to be used for any purpose other than that 
described by documents supporting the payment. 
Payments in cash should be limited only to purposes approved in Finance procedures. 
All records are to be kept and maintained by the Company for a minimum of 10 years from the date of creation, or as 
otherwise set out in the Company Document Retention Schedule approved by Group Legal from time to time. 
Incidences of Bribery and Corruption often involve some degree of inaccurate record - keeping. False, misleading or 
inaccurate books and records will not be tolerated by the Company. 
The Company requires that Employees keep accurate accounts throughout the company’s operations. 
The Company’s books, records and overall financial reporting should be transparent and should accurately reflect 
each of the underlying transactions. All expenditure should be supported by documents that accurately and properly 
describe such expenditure and the reason for the expenditure must be specifically recorded. 
In no circumstances will the Company keep parallel accounts or otherwise seek to conceal financial transactions.  
 
8. Monitoring Compliance and Reporting 
The Head of Compliance shall periodically (but not less than annually)  report on the status of Anti- Bribery and  
Corruption Compliance to the Audit and Risk Committee of the Board. Any exceptions to the general rules contained 
in the Policy should be authorised in writing by Chief Executive Officer and Head of Compliance. 
(a) Authority and Responsibility 
i. The Board is responsible for establishing this Policy and the Audit and Risk Committee of the Board is 
responsible for oversight of compliance with this Policy. 
ii. The Chief Executive Officer, supported by the Head of Compliance , has responsibility for implementing this 
Policy in accordance with the requirements of the Board. 
iii. The Heads of the Departments  are responsible for the effective implementation of this Policy in their 
respective areas and for establishing appropriate responsibilities, procedures, and internal controls to ensure 
the consistent implementation of this P olicy across all jurisdictions and compliance with its requirements.  
They are also responsible for monitoring that e mployees within their respective areas of responsibility have 
confirmed completion of ABC training. 
iv. All Employees will receive annual training on this Policy and procedures. It is the E mployee’s responsibility 
to attend such training as and when provided. See section 9 below.  
v. It is the responsibility of each E mployee and A ssociated Person to comply with this Policy.  See section 1 0 
below. 
If you see, hear or otherwise become aware of any non-compliance with ABC Laws or this Policy in the context 
of the Company’s business , it is your duty under this Policy and the Employee Code of Conduct Policy to report 
any such incident promptly and accurately. 
(b) Reporting Corruption 
Non-compliance with ABC L aws will not be tolerated, to support this, the Company is committed to ensuring  a 
safe environment where employees can report any violations, suspected violations or any issues giving rise to 
concern without fear of sanction or reprisal. 
Any suspicions of non -compliance with ABC L aws or this P olicy should be made promptly , please refer to the 
“How to report” section of the whistleblowing policy. 
Your report will be dealt with sensitively and appropriately, pursuant to the Company Whistleblower Policy.

The Audit and Risk Committee considers B ribery and Corruption risks on an ongoing basis and will assess any case 
reported. The Chief Internal Audit Officer and Head of Compliance shall review this policy regularly and at least annually 
and review the effectiveness of internal control systems at various business units  to ensure that it continues to address 
the key ABC risks faced by the Company. The results of such reviews shall be presented to the Chief Executive Officer and 
Audit and Risk Committee.  
All Employees and Associated Persons must certify that they have read and understood this Policy, either through 
records of completion maintained for the Company’s ABC training module. 
11. Monitoring and Review  
12. Certification  
The Company will monitor and review all aspects of this Policy and the control framework behind it.

ANTI-BRIBERY AND CORRUPTION POLICY – v2 SEP 2024

1. Introduction 
1.1 Dar Global PLC (“Dar Global” or "the Company" or “we” or “us”  or “the group” ) is committed to a culture of good 
business ethics and integrity and has zero tolerance of all forms of Bribery and Corruption (as defined in 4.4 below). 
The Company has a zero -tolerance approach to any of its directors, officers , employees or third parties ( in their 
relationship with the Company), being involved in Bribery or Corruption, whether by offering, promising, soliciting, 
demanding, giving or accepting a Bribe or behaving corruptly in the expectation of a Bribe or an advantage. The Policy 
is based upon Organization for Economic Co- operation and Development (OECD) Anti-Bribery Convention, United 
Nations Convention against Corruption, United Kingdom Bribery Act 2010, Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and 
other applicable anti-Bribery and Corruption legislation (ABC Laws). 
2. Objectives 
2.1 To set out the Company’s anti-Bribery and Corruption standards and provide its directors, officers, employees  and 
those who act on its behalf with clear requirements and guidelines on the prevention, detection and reporting of 
behavior in compliance with applicable ABC Laws and best practices. 
2.2 To set out the potential consequences of failure to comply with ABC Laws and the Policy. 
2.3 To further elaborate on the anti-Bribery and Corruption principles set out in the Company’s Code of Conduct Policy. 
3. Scope 
3.1 This Policy applies to: 
(a) Dar Global PLC , a company incorporated in England with registered number 14388348 and its subsidiaries  
including any future overseas developments  from time  to time and ultimately form part of  the overall 
ownership/consolidation of the Company (each a “Group Company”, collectively referred to as the “Dar Global 
Group, “Company”, “Group” ), and all directors, officers, and employees, including all consultants, contractors, 
seconded staff and casual workers wherever located (Employees); and 
(b) All of those individuals or companies who provide services to, or act for or on behalf of the Group in any capacity, 
including agents, sponsors, intermediaries, representatives, and introducers (each an Associated Person). 
 
4. Legal overview and definitions 
4.1 The Group always acts responsibly, honestly and with integrity and  has a zero -tolerance policy to any non -
compliance with ABC Laws.  
4.2 Breaches of ABC Laws or this Policy shall not be tolerated and may be considered as gross misconduct , which may 
result in a disciplinary action leading to a summary dismissal without notice and/or other legal actions. 
4.3 This Policy applies to private Bribery (i.e. where none of the persons involved are public officials), as well as Bribes 
involving Public Officials.  
4.4 For the purposes of this Policy: 
 A Bribe is anything of value given , promised, solicited  or offered with the intent to improperly influence the 
recipient or another to act in your or another’s favour , even if  authorized by management. Bribes can be money 
payments – a gift, kickback, excessive commission or other payment –  but nearly anything can be a Bribe. A Bribe 
also includes a Facilitation Payment (as defined in 5.3 below). Examples can include gifts, services, lavish travel and 
hospitality, offers of employment or internships, or any form of preferential treatment.  
 A kickback is where the bribe payer, usually the supplier of goods or services, overcharges a client, paying some or 
all of the overcharge to a representative of the client in return for being awarded a contract or continuing to receive 
business from that client, or some other business advantage. 
 Bribery is offering, promising, authorizing, giving, soliciting, seeking or accepting any financial or other advantage, 
to induce the recipient or any other person to act improperly in the performance of their functions, or to reward 
them for acting improperly, or where the recipient would act improperly by accepting the advantage.  
 Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power or position for private gain.  
 A Public Official shall be broadly interpreted and means: 
i. any elected or appointed Government official (e.g. a legislator or a member of a Government ministry); 
ii. any member of the judiciary or any person who otherwise performs a judicial or quasi-judicial function; 
iii. any employee or individual acting for or on behalf of a Government Official, a State-Owned or State-Controlled 
Enterprises, agency or enterprise performing a governmental function, a public international organization, a 
company owned or controlled in whole or in part by, a Government, (e.g. an entity hired to review bids on 
behalf of a government agency, a public University professor, etc.);

iv. any political party officer, candidate for public office, officer, or employee or individual acting for or on behalf 
of a political party or candidate for public office; 
v. any employee or individual acting for or on behalf of a public international organization (e.g. the World Bank, 
the United Nations, the European Commission);  
vi. any candidates for political offices;  
vii. any member of a royal family or a member of the military; and 
viii. any individual otherwise categorized as a Government Official under applicable law. 
 “Government” means all levels and subdivisions of governments, including local, regional, national, administrative, 
legislative or executive. 
4.5 Under the UK Bribery Act 2010, it is an offence for a corporation carrying on business (or part of a business) in the 
UK to fail to prevent Bribery including but not limited to Bribery by Employees, subsidiaries and Associated Persons. 
This applies to acts committed anywhere in the world which are intended to benefit the corporation .  The only 
defense to an offence of failing to prevent B ribery is that the corporation can demonstrate that it has “ adequate 
procedures” to prevent Bribery. 
4.6 Local laws: Almost all countries in which the Company and its subsidiaries operate have enacted ABC L aws 
criminalizing, at least, the offer of Bribes and kickbacks to Public Officials. Local laws may also impose limits on gifts, 
hospitality, and other promotional expenses. 
4.7 Key Elements: This Policy  is designed to comply with international best practices, building on the following key 
elements that are illustrated hereinafter: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4.8 Consequences of non-Compliance: The consequences of non-compliance with ABC Laws or with this Policy  may 
include imprisonment, financial penalty and/or loss of employment as listed below: 
(a) For the Company: 
• criminal or civil liabilities including unlimited fines and / or disgorgement of profits; 
• serious reputational damage including media comment; 
• debarment from tendering for public sector contracts; and 
• unenforceability of contracts entered into due to acts of Bribery, fraud or other illegality. 
(b) For Employees: 
• personal criminal liability including fines and/or imprisonment; 
• disciplinary action initiated by the Company, including summary dismissal;

(c) For Associated Persons:  
 In addition to the above, any Associated Person found to have violated the Policy or ABC Laws may be subject 
to administrative, civil or criminal liability and/or termination of the Company’s business relationship 
with such Associated Person(s). 
4.9 Your responsibilities 
You must: 
• READ and comply with this Policy. 
• Take RESPONSIBILITY for the prevention, detection and reporting of B ribery and Corruption, 
including any activity that might lead to, or suggest, a breach of this Policy. 
• REPORT as soon as possible if you believe or suspect that a breach of this Policy has occurred, or may 
occur in the future. 
 
5. Key Risk Areas and Requirements 
The Group generally prohibits the  Development, Construction and Procurement department  from accepting any Gifts 
(including promotional items) and Hospitality on an individual basis . The Procurement department may only accept to 
attend corporate events with the approval of the Group Head of Procurement where Dar Global is officially engaged as 
an organization, which would involve a group of Dar Global employees.  Other employees may accept gifts provided they 
comply with this policy. 
The Group’s second and third line s of defense (Risk, Compliance and Audit)  are not permitted to accept any g ifts, and 
may only accept nominal levels of Hospitality as described below. 
Gifts and Hospitality received by the CEO  that require manager approval will be subject to approval by the Compliance 
department. 
Below are specific situations identified that may present concern about the potential for B ribery or Corruption. 
Compliance will conduct an annual Bribery and Corruption risk assessment through interviews with key business heads 
and update this list of situations as appropriate. 
 
5.1 Gifts and Hospitality  
Employees or Associated persons acting on behalf of the C ompany may not offer, provide, request or accept Gifts or 
Hospitality from third parties (as defined below)  that could affect the receiving party’s impartiality, or influence or 
induce a business decision, e.g. 
i. Gifts / Hospitality that are excessively lavish or which are conditional on particular behaviours or 
conduct;  
ii. Gifts / Hospitality which are disproportionate to the role and means of the recipient; 
iii. Gifts /Hospitality which are used to obligate, or appear to obligate, the recipient or influence the 
recipient to act or not act in a particular way; 
iv. Gifts / Hospitality which are not provided openly and transparently; or 
v. Gifts / Hospitality whilst they are part of a tendering process directly or indirectly involving the third 
party. 
 
For these purposes:  
(a) a Gift is anything of value offered or given to an individual, a member of their family or business partner, and 
could include, for example: cash or cash equivalent (e.g. vouchers and prepaid cards), gift baskets, tickets to an 
event where the employee and third party do not attend together, travel or accommodation not connected to a 
business event, gift certificates, artwork, jewelry , electronics , offers of employment or internships , use of 
vacation facilities or hotels. 
(b) Hospitality is an event to which you accompany a third party, and could include, for example, a meal, sports 
match, event or concert and any travelling, accommodation and refreshments (if you do not accompany the third 
party, the Hospitality should be treated as a Gift).

Employees must register (see 5.4) and seek written approval for Gifts or Hospitality received or provided as required 
by the guidelines set out below. The conditions for acceptance and approval requirements for providing; and receiving 
Gifts and Hospitality, from business contacts and public officials are set out below.  
 
Employees are strictly prohibited from: 
• Requesting gifts from third parties; 
• Accepting cash or a cash equivalent (such as gift vouchers, certificates with a set negotiable value); 
• Accepting any gift of a value over $50 (although the offer and refusal of that gift should be recorded through 
the gifts register); 
• Giving or receiving any gift other than promotional items, to a public official; 
• Accepting gifts of any kind during a tendering process or in any other circumstances where it could give the 
appearance of being given to influence a business decision;  
• Accepting any gift in circumstances where the receipt would or could appear to be improper.  
 
In order to ensure transparency and oversight, employees must record all offered gifts of a more than nominal value 
(promotional items of less than $15) on our centralized gifts register whether they have been accepted or declined. 
In assessing the value of the gift offered, employees are required to take a sensible approach, which may include an 
internet search if the value is not immediately clear. 
 
Employees should refuse any gift offered which is valued at more than $50. The only exception to this is where the 
gift was intended and is capable of being shared between the team – such as a case of wine or gift basket containing 
multiple items where the division of the gift between team members would result in each team member accepting a 
gift of less than $50. Consent from the line manager must be sought and such a gift recorded on the register. Where 
a gift requires consent from a line manager and/or entry on the gift register, this ought to be done as soon as possible 
and in any event within five working days.  
 
Employees must submit all expense claims relating to gifts provided to third parties in accordance with our expenses 
policy and record the reason for expenditure on the gift register. All accounts, invoices, and other records relating to 
dealings with third parties including suppliers and customers should be prepared with strict accuracy and 
completeness. Accounts must not be kept “off-book” to facilitate or conceal improper payments.

Hospitality may be given or received as part of the development and maintenance of healthy and productive working 
relationships with our clients and partners, however it is important that employees consider the context in which 
hospitality is provided to e nsure that it could not be perceived as an attempt to influence the judgement of the 
recipient improperly, or impact how they perform their functions.  
 
Employees, in deciding whether to give or receive hospitality should consider: 
• How frequently the hospitality has been given or received –  has this client been taken for dinner at a much 
greater frequency than others? 
• Is there an active tender or decision being made which would make the provision or receipt of hospitality 
inappropriate? Could it give the appearance of impropriety?  
• Is the value of the hospitality being offered such that it gives the appearance of impropriety?  
• Has there been any suggestion that the hospitality is kept ‘off the books’? 
 
Employees are strictly prohibited from: 
• Requesting hospitality from third parties; 
• Accepting hospitality provided from a third party whilst they are part of a tendering process  directly or 
indirectly involving the third party; 
• Giving or accepting hospitality which would cause embarrassment to the company by virtue of the activity 
offered or the venue in which it was provided; 
• Giving any hospitality to public officials, or accepting more than nominal hospitality (such as refreshments 
during meetings) from public officials; 
• Accepting or receiving any hospitality which may create an appearance of impropriety.  
 
In order to ensure transparency and oversight, employees must record hospitality in line with the requirements set 
out below on our a uthorizing gifts register. The employee should set out the client, the reason for the hospitality, 
type and value and any material considerations for the supervisor as set out above. 
 
Where employees are required to seek line manager approval, they are required to do so in advance of receiving the 
hospitality, or where this is not possible, within five business days. Dar Global has set a reasonable cap on the giving 
and receiving of hospitality for business development purposes at $200 per person. In extraordinary circumstances, 
where hospitality is likely to exceed $200, employees must seek prior consent from the Group CEO setting out the 
nature, purpose and estimated value of the hospitality. This must be recorded on the hospitality register.   
 
A failure to seek consent and record hospitality where required is a breach of this policy and may result in 
disciplinary action. As such, appropriate planning should be conducted by those involved in engagement with third 
parties such as  Government Relations,  Business Development, Human Resources  and Procurement/Contractor 
management to anticipate and pre-authorise potential hospitality scenarios. 
 
Employees must submit all expenses claims relating to hospitality provided to third parties in accordance with our 
expenses policy and record the reason for expenditure. All accounts, invoices, and other records relating to dealings 
with third parties incl uding suppliers and customers should be prepared with strict accuracy and completeness. 
Accounts must not be kept “off-book” to facilitate or conceal improper payments.
